shape.subject: Mathematics
shape.scope: Numbers and their operations (primes, HCF/LCM, squares/cubes/roots, standard form, estimation, significant figures); ratio and proportion (incl. map scales, direct and inverse proportion); percentage (incl. reverse percentage); rate and speed (incl. average speed, conversion of units); financial mathematics (simple and compound interest, hire purchase, money exchange, taxation, utilities bills); algebraic expressions and formulae (expansion, factorisation incl. grouping and quadratic trinomials, algebraic fractions, changing the subject, algebraic identities); functions and graphs (linear, quadratic incl. completed-square and factorised forms, cubic, reciprocal y=a/x and a/x^2, exponential y=ka^x, drawing on a grid from a table of values, gradient of a curve by a tangent, solving equations by drawing a suitable line); equations and inequalities (linear, simultaneous linear, quadratic by factorisation / completing the square / the formula, fractional equations reducing to quadratics, linear inequalities incl. double inequalities, word problems leading to these); set language and notation (union, intersection, complement, subsets, Venn diagrams with numbers of elements); matrices (display of information, addition, scalar multiplication, multiplication of two matrices, interpretation of the product; no inverses); problems in real-world contexts (reading tables and information sheets, making and justifying a decision, estimating a cost or a quantity); angles, triangles and polygons (angle properties of parallel lines, triangles, quadrilaterals and regular polygons; construction with ruler, compasses and protractor: perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors; scale drawings); congruence and similarity (tests, ratios of lengths, areas and volumes of similar figures and solids); properties of circles (symmetry properties: equal chords, perpendicular from centre, tangents from a point; angle properties: angle at centre, angle in a semicircle, angles in the same segment, opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral, tangent-radius; reasons stated); Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry (sine, cosine and tangent for acute and obtuse angles, sine and cosine rules, area of a triangle as ½ab sin C, bearings, angles of elevation and depression, simple 3-D problems); mensuration (area of a triangle, parallelogram, trapezium, circle; arc length and sector area with the angle in RADIANS or degrees; surface area and volume of a prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone and sphere; composite solids); coordinate geometry (gradient, length, midpoint is NOT required, equation of a straight line y=mx+c, parallel lines, area of a rectilinear figure by shoelace is NOT required — use base×height or split into triangles); vectors in two dimensions (column vectors, magnitude, position vectors, addition, scalar multiples, collinearity, expressing one vector in terms of others, ratios of areas of triangles with a common height or on the same base); data handling and analysis (tables, bar charts, pie charts, pictograms, line graphs, histograms with equal class widths, dot diagrams, stem-and-leaf, box-and-whisker plots, cumulative frequency curves, median, quartiles, percentiles, range, interquartile range, mean and standard deviation for grouped and ungrouped data, comparing two distributions in context); probability (single events, combined events by possibility diagrams and tree diagrams, with and without replacement, mutually exclusive and independent events). NOT in 4052: calculus, logarithms, surds, the binomial theorem, trigonometric identities, the R-formula, quadratic inequalities, matrices inverses and determinants, vectors in three dimensions, the shoelace formula, the midpoint formula.
shape.register:
REGISTER — how SEAB asks (4052)
- Plain, exact, economical English. Instructions are imperatives: Find, Calculate, Work out, Write down, Simplify, Factorise, Expand, Solve, Show that, Explain why, Give a reason, Complete the table, Draw, Describe, Estimate, Express, State.
- Parts are labelled (a), (b), (c), with sub-parts (i), (ii). Every part carries its marks. A 1–3 mark question is often a single unlabelled part.
- A scientific calculator is allowed on BOTH papers. Never write "a calculator must not be used". The paper's rubric already says: non-exact answers to 3 significant figures, angles to 1 decimal place, π = calculator value or 3.142 — so a question states a precision only when it wants something else ("correct to 2 decimal places", "in its simplest form", "in terms of π", "as a fraction in its lowest terms", "in standard form", "to the nearest cent").
- Angles are in DEGREES with the degree sign ($58^\circ$); a sector angle in radians is stated as "1.8 radians". Bearings are three-figure ($048^\circ$). Money is dollars and cents ($\$92.75$).
- Contexts are short, concrete and Singaporean-neutral (a garden fountain, a box of apples, a map of Singapore, a candle business): the situation in one or two sentences, units given, then the parts. Never chatty, never a story.
- "Show that" states its target exactly ("Show that $x^2 - 102x + 1440 = 0$", "Show that $p = 2.5$") and a later part uses it. "Explain why …" / "Give a reason for your answer" / "Is he correct?" parts are worth 1 mark and expect one sentence with a number in it. A circle-properties question says "Give a reason for each step of your working."
- Statistics and probability parts ask for interpretation in context ("By commenting on the means and the standard deviations, compare …", "Explain what this tells you about …").
- Paper 1 (27 short questions, 90 marks): each question tests ONE idea in 1–7 marks, answered in the space provided; the paper walks the syllabus (number, algebra, geometry, statistics interleaved), with the vector and mensuration questions near the end.
- Paper 2 (9 long questions, 90 marks): each question is 8–12 marks in 3–5 parts. Early questions are ALGEBRA MEDLEYS whose parts (a), (b), (c), (d) are separate short problems on different algebra skills. Later ones are one context developed through parts: a graph question (a table of values with two blanks, "On the grid, draw the graph of …", a gradient by a tangent, "By drawing a suitable straight line, solve …"), a trigonometry-on-the-ground question with bearings and a mast, a statistics + probability question over a table or histogram, a circle-properties + circular-measure question, a speed/quadratic question ("Show that … = 0", solve to 2 decimal places, reject a root, interpret), and the last question is a PROBLEM IN A REAL-WORLD CONTEXT: an information sheet (a table of prices, rates or measurements) followed by parts that end in a 5–7 mark "Suggest a suitable … Justify your answer" or "Is it worth …? Show your working" decision.
- Marks follow the work: about 1 mark per 1.5 minutes. 1 mark: read/state/one-line. 2 marks: one routine. 3–4 marks: a short chain. 5–7 marks: a multi-step argument or a decision with working.

title: E Math · Set 1 · Paper 1 · O-Level format

question.stem:
The mean of five numbers is $m$.
Four of the numbers are $x$, $2x - 3$, $x + 7$ and $3x$.
Find an expression, in terms of $m$ and $x$, for the fifth number.
Give your answer in its simplest form.
question.solution:
The five numbers have mean $m$, so their sum is $5m$.
Sum of the four given numbers $= x + (2x - 3) + (x + 7) + 3x = 7x + 4$.
Fifth number $= 5m - (7x + 4) = 5m - 7x - 4$.

Marking: M1 for $5m - (x + 2x - 3 + x + 7 + 3x)$, i.e. recognising the total is $5m$ and subtracting the four; A1 for $5m - 7x - 4$. The answer $m - 7x - 4$ (total taken as $m$) scores M0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Algebraic expressions and formulae: forming an expression from a verbal statement and simplifying by collecting like terms; the mean is used only as its definition (sum = mean x count). No content outside 4052.
question.originality_note: New situation and structure: the hidden operation is that the total is $5m$, not $m$, which the candidate must supply. It is not a bare 'simplify' (GCE 2024 P1 Q1), not a parity argument (GCE 2025 P1 Q12), not a completed-square equivalence (GCE 2023 P1 Q6), not a units expression (GCE 2011 P1 Q5), and no corpus question asks for a missing number in terms of a mean.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter 5m - 7x - 4; blind examiner 5m - 7x - 4. Verified: sum of the four = x + 2x - 3 + x + 7 + 3x = 7x + 4; total = 5m; fifth = 5m - (7x + 4).

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement; the key 5m - 7x - 4 is correct and the M0 trap m - 7x - 4 is rightly identified.
verdict.why: A genuine 2-mark opener at the 2024/25 standard: one hidden operation the candidate must supply (the total is 5m, not m) with a tidy-looking wrong answer (m - 7x - 4), then routine collection of terms; register matches GCE exactly (GCE 2023 P1 Q10: 'Find p in terms of q. Give your answer in its simplest form.'). Not a re-skin: GCE 2024 P1 Q21 uses a mean to reach a quadratic 'show that', GCE 2024 P1 Q8 is an arithmetic sequence, GCE 2015 P1 Q3 is a numeric mean/median/mode puzzle; no corpus item asks for a missing number as an expression in the mean. Gates: pass.

question.stem:
A sector of a circle has radius 7.5 cm and arc length 12 cm.
A second sector has the same angle as the first sector.
The area of the second sector is four times the area of the first sector.
Calculate the perimeter of the second sector.
question.solution:
Method 1 (scale factor). The two sectors have the same angle, so they are similar. Four times the area means the length scale factor is $\sqrt{4} = 2$.
Radius of the second sector $= 2 \times 7.5 = 15$ cm and its arc length $= 2 \times 12 = 24$ cm.
Perimeter $= 15 + 15 + 24 = 54$ cm.

Method 2 (through the angle). Arc length $s = r\theta$ gives $\theta = \dfrac{12}{7.5} = 1.6$ radians.
Area of the first sector $= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 7.5^2 \times 1.6 = 45$ cm$^2$, so the area of the second sector is $4 \times 45 = 180$ cm$^2$.
$\dfrac{1}{2} r^2 \times 1.6 = 180$, so $r^2 = 225$ and $r = 15$ cm.
Arc length of the second sector $= 15 \times 1.6 = 24$ cm.
Perimeter $= 2 \times 15 + 24 = 54$ cm.

Marking: M1 for the length scale factor 2, or for $r = 15$ (or arc $= 24$) obtained through the areas; A1 for 54 cm. The tidy wrong route (scaling the lengths by 4: radius 30 cm, arc 48 cm, perimeter 108 cm) scores M0. An answer of 24 cm (arc only) or 39 cm (one radius) scores M1 A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Mensuration: arc length $s = r\theta$ and sector area $\frac{1}{2} r^2 \theta$ with the angle in radians (radian measure is in the 4052 syllabus, as at GCE 2023 P1 Q2(b), GCE 2024 P2 Q8(a)(ii) and GCE 2025 P2 Q6(a)); 4052 Congruence and similarity: ratio of areas of similar figures. No content outside 4052.
question.originality_note: No figure, no shaded region, no wiper (GCE 2024 P1 Q9), no degree-radian conversion (GCE 2023 P1 Q2), no quadrant-plus-semicircle perimeter (GCE 2008 P1 Q6), no sector area after angle chasing (GCE 2025 P1 Q16(c)). One unlabelled 2-mark item: the candidate must decide that four times the area means a length scale factor of 2 (the tidy wrong answer is 108 cm), then the routine perimeter; nothing hands over the angle, and every datum is used. No corpus question combines a given arc with an area scaling to a perimeter.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give 54 cm. Checked two ways: same angle so the sectors are similar, area x4 gives length scale factor 2, radius 15, arc 24, perimeter 15+15+24 = 54 (or 2 x 27). Through the angle: theta = 12/7.5 = 1.6 rad, A1 = 1/2 x 7.5^2 x 1.6 = 45, A2 = 180, r^2 = 225, r = 15, arc 24, perimeter 54. A degrees route (theta ~ 91.67 deg) also gives 54, so the item does not even depend on radians; radian arc/sector work is in the 4052 syllabus in any case (GCE 2024 P2 Q8(a)(ii), GCE 2025 P2 Q6(a), GCE 2023 P1 Q2(b)).

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner both give 54 cm; the key is correct and the mark scheme (M1 scale factor 2 or r = 15, A1 54; the x4-on-lengths route 108 cm scores M0) is sound.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 two-mark standard: exactly one idea is the candidate's (the area ratio 4 becomes a length ratio 2, or the same fact reached through the angle) and the rest is a short routine, about three minutes; the tidy wrong decision (scaling lengths by 4) gives 108 cm, so the trap is real. Register, precision and the numbers (1.6, 45, 180, 225) are exam-clean, the round-1 ladder is gone, gates pass (nearest neighbour Jaccard 0.071), and no 2024/25 P1 item shares the situation - the nearest structures, GCE 2025 P1 Q21(b) (volume ratio in a cone) and GCE 2025 P1 Q9 (cube TSA to volume), are different figures and different mechanisms. A 2-mark radian item at Q2 has precedent (GCE 2023 P1 Q2).

question.stem:
Priya buys a refrigerator on hire purchase.
She pays a deposit of one quarter of the cash price, followed by 18 equal monthly payments of $\$170$.
The total amount she pays is $10\%$ more than the cash price of the refrigerator.
Calculate the cash price of the refrigerator.
question.solution:
Let the cash price be $\$C$.
Deposit $= \dfrac{1}{4}C$. The monthly payments total $18 \times 170 = \$3060$.
Total amount paid $= \dfrac{1}{4}C + 3060$.
The total amount paid is $110\%$ of the cash price, so
$\dfrac{1}{4}C + 3060 = 1.1C$
$3060 = 1.1C - 0.25C = 0.85C$
$C = \dfrac{3060}{0.85} = 3600$.
The cash price is $\$3600$.
Check: deposit $\$900$, payments $\$3060$, total $\$3960 = 1.1 \times 3600$.

Marking: M1 for expressing both the deposit and the total in terms of the cash price and equating, e.g. $\frac{1}{4}C + 3060 = 1.1C$, or the equivalent statement that the 18 payments make up $110\% - 25\% = 85\%$ of the cash price; M1 for $0.85C = 3060$ or $\dfrac{3060}{0.85}$; A1 for $\$3600$. The tidy wrong routes all score M0: ignoring the $10\%$ and taking the payments as $75\%$ of the cash price gives $\dfrac{3060}{0.75} = \$4080$; taking $3060$ as $90\%$ or $110\%$ of the cash price gives $\$3400$ or $\$2781.82$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Financial mathematics (hire purchase: a deposit plus equal monthly instalments; the hire-purchase price compared with the cash price) and Percentage (a quantity expressed as a percentage more than an unknown, i.e. reverse percentage), solved through a linear equation in one unknown (4052 Equations: linear equations with the unknown on both sides). No content outside 4052.
question.originality_note: Not the GCE 2024 P1 Q3 shell: no cash price is given, there is no (a) 'total paid' part and no (b) 'extra cost as a percentage'; the item is a single unlabelled 3-mark question whose unknown is the cash price, which sits on BOTH sides of an equation the candidate must form (deposit as a quarter of it, total as 110% of it). The corpus hire-purchase questions all start from a stated cash price (GCE 2024 P1 Q3, GCE 2015 P2 Q3, GCE 2013 P2 Q2, GCE 2023 specimen P2 Q2, GCE 2010 P2 Q3) or a stated cash AND hire-purchase price (GCE 2014 P1 Q11 asks the monthly payment, GCE 2018 P1 Q8 the deposit as a percentage); none asks for the cash price and none needs an equation with the unknown on both sides. New context (a refrigerator), an 18-month term no exemplar uses, a quarter deposit, new numbers. At the 2024/25 standard: the one decision is the model $\frac{1}{4}C + 3060 = 1.1C$ (no 'form an equation' cue), the routine is a two-step linear solve, and the wrong decisions land on tidy-looking answers ($\$4080$, $\$3400$).

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement; $3600 is right and the mark scheme (M1 model or the 85% statement, M1 0.85C = 3060, A1) is sound.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 standard for [3]: the one idea the candidate must supply is the model (the 18 payments are 110% - 25% = 85% of the cash price, or C/4 + 3060 = 1.1C) with no 'form an equation' cue, and the rest is a two-step routine finishable well inside 4.5 minutes; the wrong decisions give tidy-looking answers (4080 if the 10% is ignored, 3400 or 2781.82 with the wrong base) and the numbers are examination-clean. It is not a re-skin: GCE 2024 P1 Q3 is the forward two-part ladder (cash price given, compute the total then the extra as a %) with no decision, while this is the unscaffolded reverse problem asking for the one unknown no corpus HP item asks for (2014 P1 Q11 the payment, 2018 P1 Q8 the deposit %, 2024 P1 Q3 the total and the extra %); hire purchase recurring as a situation is how SEAB itself reuses it across years. Register and mark discipline read as SEAB's ('plus' in place of 'followed by' would match their cadence exactly but is cosmetic). Gates: pass, jaccard 0.124 to GCE 2024 P1 Q3, nothing to list.

question.stem:
The ages, in years, of the six members of a band are listed in ascending order.
$18 \qquad 21 \qquad 24 \qquad x \qquad 30 \qquad 31$
The median age of the six members is 26 years.
Two more people, aged 25 years and 33 years, join the band.
Find the median age of the eight members.
question.solution:
For six values in ascending order, the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th values.
$\frac{24 + x}{2} = 26$, so $24 + x = 52$ and $x = 28$.
(Check: $24 \le 28 \le 30$, so the list is in ascending order.)

The eight ages in ascending order are $18, 21, 24, 25, 28, 30, 31, 33$.
For eight values, the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th values.
Median $= \frac{25 + 28}{2} = 26.5$ years.

Marking: M1 for $x = 28$ (or for the equation $\frac{24 + x}{2} = 26$); A1 for 26.5. The newcomer aged 25 sits between 24 and $x$, so the median does not stay at 26 and the value of $x$ is needed: 28 (copying $x$), 26 (assuming one age below and one above leaves the median unchanged), 25 (the 4th of eight, or the median of the seven known ages) and 29 (the mean of the two newcomers) all score A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Statistics: median of ungrouped data with an even number of values, applied twice. The value of $x$ comes from an equation the candidate forms from the definition of the median (no 'form an equation' cue), then the two newcomers must be placed in the ordered list and the 4th and 5th of eight identified. No figure, no content outside 4052.
question.originality_note: New situation and structure: an unknown inside an ordered list is fixed by the median, then two newcomers change which positions the median uses. The answer, 26.5, is neither $x$ nor any median stated in the question, so it cannot be reached by copying $x$ or by a 'newcomer = median' shortcut, and every shortcut gives a tidy but distinct wrong answer (28, 26, 25, 29). Not a box-and-whisker reading, a pie chart, a grouped table or a mean/SD comparison; unlike Q1 of this paper (an expression for a missing value from a MEAN), this tests the positional definition of the median and re-ordering after values are added. The nearest corpus kin, GCE 2024 P1 Q21(a), uses the mean and a 3-mark show-that.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter and blind examiner both give 26.5 years. Verified independently: for six values in ascending order the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th, so (24 + x)/2 = 26 gives x = 28 (24 <= 28 <= 30, list stays ascending); the eight ages in order are 18, 21, 24, 25, 28, 30, 31, 33 and the median is (25 + 28)/2 = 26.5. Unique, well-posed, correct.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on the single answer 26.5 years and both are right; nothing in the key is disputed.
fixes: Present the six ages as a displayed list on its own line, SEAB house style for raw data (GCE 2024 P1 Q8: 'w  15  x  y  z'; GCE 2024 P1 Q21: '12  24  8  21  28  17  2p  4p^2'), with the sentence above it: 'The ages, in years, of the six members of a band are listed in ascending order.' then '18   21   24   x   30   31' — rather than running the list inside the sentence.
Wording: 'Two more people, aged 25 years and 33 years, join the band.' — they are not members until they join; the current 'Two more members ... join' reads slightly off in SEAB register.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 2-mark P1 standard: x is hidden behind the even-count median with no 'form an equation' cue, the newcomers must be re-ordered into the list and the 25 lands between the original middle pair so the tidy 'one below, one above, median unchanged' answer 26 is wrong (the standard's 2-mark shape: one routine with a re-ordering or hidden operation, one idea then routine, finishable well inside 3 minutes); the round-1 defect (a (b) answer coinciding with x and the stated median) is gone. Not a re-skin of any exemplar or 2024/25 P1 item (nearest kin GCE 2024 P1 Q21(a), a mean show-that with a quadratic, and GCE 2024 P1 Q8, an arithmetic sequence from a stated sum); all gates pass (novelty nearest GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q5, Jaccard 0.02). Only light register edits stand between it and a real paper.

question.stem:
Lim has $\$5000$ to invest for 2 years.
Bank A pays simple interest at $3.5\%$ per year.
Bank B pays compound interest at $4\%$ per year.
Calculate how much more interest Lim earns in the second year with Bank B than with Bank A.
question.solution:
Bank A pays the same interest every year: $\frac{5000 \times 3.5}{100} = \$175$ in the second year (or $\frac{5000 \times 3.5 \times 2}{100} \div 2 = 350 \div 2 = 175$).
Bank B: amount at the end of the first year $= 5000 \times 1.04 = \$5200$.
The second year's interest is $4\%$ of $\$5200$: $5200 \times 0.04 = \$208$.
(Equivalently $5000 \times 1.04^2 - 5000 \times 1.04 = 5408 - 5200 = 208$.)
Difference $= 208 - 175 = \$33$.
Mark scheme: M1 for Bank A's yearly interest $175$ (or $350 \div 2$); M1 for $5200 \times 0.04$ or $5408 - 5200$ (the year-2 interest on the compounded amount); A1 for $\$33$.
Tidy wrong answers: $\$25$ (from $5000 \times 0.04 - 175$, using $\$5000$ as the base in year 2) and $\$58$ (from $408 - 350$, the two-year totals).
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Financial mathematics: simple interest and compound interest, in one unscaffolded 3-mark question. The candidate must isolate ONE year's interest for each bank himself: for Bank A that simple interest is the same every year (175), and for Bank B that the second year's interest is 4% of the amount after one year (5200), or the difference between the amounts after two years and after one year — not 4% of the principal and not the two-year total. One decision (the compounding base for year 2), then a two-step routine. Money to the cent; all answers exact.
question.originality_note: New situation and new question: two banks, and the comparison is confined to the SECOND year of interest, which forces the compounding base to be chosen. Set as a single 3-mark question with no parts, as 2024/25 P1 does (GCE 2024 P1 Q16, GCE 2025 P1 Q3 are both single-part), so no lead-in hands the candidate Bank A's side. The corpus compares simple and compound only over the whole period (GCE 2003 P2 Q1(a)(ii), 3 years total; GCE 2022 P2 Q2(a), an explain), reverses from total interest (GCE 2024 P1 Q16, 2017 P1 Q13), finds r (2020 P1 Q15) or explains monthly compounding (2023 P1 Q5). No corpus item asks for the interest of one specified later year.

answers.single: $33 (Bank B second-year interest = 0.04 x 5200 = $208; Bank A second-year interest = 0.035 x 5000 = $175; 208 - 175 = $33)

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give $33. Worked independently: Bank A earns 5000 x 0.035 = $175 in any year; Bank B's amount after year 1 is 5000 x 1.04 = $5200, so its year-2 interest is 5200 x 0.04 = $208 (= 5408 - 5200); 208 - 175 = 33. Correct. The setter's tidy wrong answers are real: $25 (year-2 base taken as 5000) and $58 (two-year totals 408 - 350).

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on the single answer $33 and both are right; nothing in the key is disputed.
verdict.why: Round 1's one fix (drop the scaffolding (a) that handed over Bank A's side) has been applied: this is now one unscaffolded 3-mark question in which the candidate must decide the compounding base for the second year (5200, not 5000, not the two-year totals - both misreads give tidy wrong answers), then run a two-step routine, which is exactly the 2024/25 3-mark shape; register, numbers and syllabus scope are clean, gates pass, and it re-skins no 2024/25 P1 item (GCE 2024 P1 Q16 reverses from total interest, GCE 2025 P1 Q3 is a simple-interest total; no corpus item isolates one later year's interest).

question.stem: A map of a nature reserve has a scale of $1 : 20\,000$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text:
A trail in the nature reserve is 2.4 km long.
Calculate the length, in centimetres, of the trail on the map.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
A reservoir in the nature reserve has an area of $50$ cm$^2$ on this map.
The same reservoir is shown on a second map with a scale of $1 : 50\,000$.
Calculate the area, in square centimetres, of the reservoir on the second map.

question.solution:
(a) $2.4$ km $= 2.4 \times 100\,000 = 240\,000$ cm.
Length on the map $= \frac{240\,000}{20\,000} = 12$ cm.

(b) Method 1 (through the actual area): on the first map $1$ cm represents $20\,000$ cm $= 0.2$ km, so $1$ cm$^2$ represents $0.2^2 = 0.04$ km$^2$ and the actual area of the reservoir is $50 \times 0.04 = 2$ km$^2$.
On the second map $1$ cm represents $0.5$ km, so $1$ cm$^2$ represents $0.5^2 = 0.25$ km$^2$; area on the second map $= \frac{2}{0.25} = 8$ cm$^2$.
Method 2 (ratio of the scales): the second map draws every length at $\frac{20\,000}{50\,000} = \frac{2}{5}$ of its length on the first map, so every area is multiplied by $\left(\frac{2}{5}\right)^2 = \frac{4}{25}$.
Area $= 50 \times \frac{4}{25} = 8$ cm$^2$.
Mark scheme: M1 for squaring the length factor (either route, i.e. $\times \frac{4}{25}$, or $\times 0.04$ then $\div 0.25$ correctly ordered); A1 for $8$.
Tidy wrong answers: $50 \times \frac{2}{5} = 20$ cm$^2$ (scaling the area by the length factor); $50 \times \frac{25}{4} = 312.5$ cm$^2$ (the factor inverted).
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Ratio and proportion: map scales, converting actual lengths to map lengths (km to cm), and the area scale factor as the square of the length scale factor. Part (b) requires the candidate to decide that a change of map scale multiplies areas by the square of the ratio of the scales, and which way the factor goes. All answers exact; no figure needed (the map is not drawn).
question.originality_note: New situation (a nature reserve, a reservoir drawn on two maps of different scales) and a structure not in the corpus: every corpus map-scale item converts between one map and the ground (GCE 2024 P1 Q6, 2020 P1 Q17, 2016 P1 Q20, 2011/2012 P1, 2003 P1 Q14), derives a scale from measured lengths or an area (GCE 2025 P2 Q3(b), 2019 P1 Q23(a)) or is a scale drawing with bearings. Converting an area from one map to another of a different scale, where the tempting error is a linear factor, is new. The scale pair (1 : 20 000 and 1 : 50 000) and the feature (a reservoir) are deliberately away from GCE 2011 P1 Q9's 1 : 25 000 map and lake, and no shown exemplar uses either scale.

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 12 cm: 2.4 km = 240 000 cm, divided by 20 000. Correct.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 8 cm^2. Checked both routes: length factor 20 000/50 000 = 2/5, area factor 4/25, 50 x 4/25 = 8; or 1 cm^2 on the first map = 0.04 km^2 so the reservoir is 2 km^2, and 1 cm^2 on the second map = 0.25 km^2, 2/0.25 = 8. Correct. The linear-factor slip gives the tidy 20 and the inverted factor 312.5, as the setter says.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on both parts and both are right; nothing in the key is disputed.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 standard for 3 marks at Q6: (a) is the 1-mark conversion the real Q6 also opens with (GCE 2024 P1 Q6(a)/(b)), and (b) makes the candidate supply the one idea (square the ratio of the two scales, and point it the right way, since the second map is the smaller scale) before a one-line routine, with 20 cm^2 waiting for the linear-factor slip, the same weight as GCE 2024 P1 Q6(c) [2]. question.stem: Show all your construction lines and arcs clearly.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Using ruler and compasses only, construct triangle $ABC$ in which $AB = 8$ cm, $AC = 6$ cm and $BC = 6.5$ cm.
parts.answer: Line $AB = 8.0$ cm drawn; arcs of radius $6$ cm centred $A$ and radius $6.5$ cm centred $B$ shown crossing at $C$; triangle completed with $AC = 6.0$ cm and $BC = 6.5$ cm (each side within $\pm 0.1$ cm).

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The point $P$ lies inside the triangle.
$P$ is the same distance from $A$ as it is from $B$, and the same distance from $AB$ as it is from $AC$.
Using ruler and compasses only, construct and label the point $P$.
parts.answer: Perpendicular bisector of $AB$ constructed with its arcs shown [1]; bisector of angle $BAC$ constructed with its arcs shown [1]; $P$ labelled where the two lines cross, $2.0$ cm directly above the midpoint of $AB$ (so $PA = PB = 4.5$ cm).

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: By measuring, find the shortest distance from $P$ to $AC$.
parts.answer: $2.0$ cm (exact value $4\tan 26.51^\circ = 1.995$ cm; accept $1.8$ to $2.2$ cm, i.e. $\pm 0.2$ cm, because $P$ is fixed by two constructions built on the candidate's own triangle). Follow through from the candidate's own correctly constructed $P$ (ft their $P$).

question.solution:
(a) Draw $AB = 8$ cm. With centre $A$ and radius $6$ cm draw an arc above $AB$; with centre $B$ and radius $6.5$ cm draw an arc to cut it. The crossing is $C$; join $AC$ and $BC$. Check by the cosine rule: $\cos A = \frac{6^2 + 8^2 - 6.5^2}{2 \times 6 \times 8} = \frac{57.75}{96} = \frac{77}{128}$, so angle $BAC = 53.02^\circ$, angle $ABC = 47.51^\circ$, angle $ACB = 79.47^\circ$, and $C$ is $6 \sin 53.02^\circ = 4.79$ cm above $AB$. The drawing is $8$ cm wide and under $5$ cm tall, so it fits the answer space with room for arcs below $AB$.

(b) $P$ is the same distance from $A$ as from $B$, so $P$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $AB$: with one compass opening (more than $4$ cm) draw arcs centred $A$ and centred $B$ that cross above and below $AB$, and join the two crossings; this line meets $AB$ at its midpoint $M$, $4$ cm from $A$. $P$ is the same distance from the lines $AB$ and $AC$, so $P$ lies on the bisector of angle $BAC$: with centre $A$ draw an arc cutting $AB$ and $AC$, from the two cuts draw equal arcs crossing inside the angle, and join $A$ to the crossing. $P$ is the point where the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ meets the bisector of angle $BAC$. Exactly: the bisector makes an angle $\frac{1}{2} \times 53.02^\circ = 26.51^\circ$ with $AB$, and $\tan 26.51^\circ = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos A}{1 + \cos A}} = \sqrt{\frac{51}{205}} = 0.4988$, so $PM = 4 \tan 26.51^\circ = 1.995$ cm and $PA = PB = \frac{4}{\cos 26.51^\circ} = 4.47$ cm. $P$ is inside the triangle: directly above $M$ the side $BC$ is $4.79 \times \frac{8 - 4}{8 - 3.61} = 4.37$ cm above $AB$, while $P$ is $1.995$ cm above $AB$; and the bisector of angle $A$ reaches $BC$ at $\frac{2 \times 6 \times 8 \cos 26.51^\circ}{6 + 8} = 6.14$ cm from $A$, beyond $P$.

(c) Because $P$ lies on the bisector of angle $BAC$, its shortest distance from $AC$ equals its shortest distance from $AB$; and the perpendicular bisector already drawn is perpendicular to $AB$, so that distance is simply $PM$, read off the drawing: $PM = 1.995 = 2.0$ cm. A candidate who instead constructs the perpendicular from $P$ to $AC$ measures the same $2.0$ cm. Accept $1.8$ to $2.2$ cm, follow through from their $P$ (a $1^\circ$ slip in the angle bisector alone moves $PM$ to $1.91$ or $2.08$ cm).
question.syllabus_check: 4052 G1 Angles, triangles and polygons: construction of a triangle from three given sides with ruler and compasses; construction of the perpendicular bisector of a line segment and the bisector of an angle; the perpendicular bisector as the set of points equidistant from two points and the angle bisector as the set of points equidistant from two lines; measurement of a length with a ruler. No printed figure, no scale drawing, no loci beyond these two bisectors.
question.originality_note: Self-contained: the triangle is constructed from three stated sides, so nothing depends on a printed figure and nothing is measured from one. Unlike GCE 2025 P1 Q7, GCE 2019 P1 Q12, GCE 2017 P1 Q10 and the GCE 2023 specimen Q7 (each names the two constructions on a printed quadrilateral or triangle and then shades a region or marks a point), neither construction here is named: each condition is an equal-distance statement the candidate must decode into the right bisector. Unlike GCE 2011 P1 Q20 (side AB pre-drawn, the two constructions named in (b), a region-type point in (c)), the point P is fixed by the two hidden loci and the last mark is a shortest distance to a line whose value the bisector property lets the candidate read straight off the perpendicular bisector already drawn. Scalene triangle with angles 53.0, 47.5 and 79.5 degrees, no special angle, no region shading, no scale.

answers.(a): Triangle ABC constructed: draw base AB = 8 cm with a ruler; with centre A and compass radius 6 cm draw an arc above AB; with centre B and compass radius 6.5 cm draw a second arc cutting the first at C; join AC and BC (arcs left showing). Construction is well-defined and possible: 6 + 6.5 = 12.5 > 8, so the arcs intersect (angle BAC = 53.0 deg).
answers.(b): P = intersection of (i) the perpendicular bisector of AB (locus of points equidistant from A and B: equal arcs from A and from B, radius more than half of AB, above and below AB, joined) and (ii) the bisector of angle BAC (locus of points equidistant from AB and AC: arc centred at A cutting AB and AC, then equal arcs from those two crossing points, joined to A). The two loci meet at exactly one point, which lies inside the triangle, so P is well-defined; label it P. (P is 4 cm from A along AB's perpendicular bisector, i.e. 2.00 cm above the midpoint of AB.)
answers.(c): 2.0 cm (perpendicular from P to AC; exact value 1.995 cm, so accept 1.9 - 2.1 cm)

working.(a): Ruler-and-compasses: (1) rule AB = 8.0 cm. (2) Compasses set to 6.0 cm, centre A, arc above AB. (3) Compasses set to 6.5 cm, centre B, arc above AB cutting the first arc at C. (4) Rule AC and BC. Possible because the triangle inequality holds for 8, 6, 6.5 (6 + 6.5 = 12.5 > 8; 8 + 6 > 6.5; 8 + 6.5 > 6), so the two arcs genuinely intersect. All construction arcs are left on the diagram.
working.(b): Two loci: locus 1 = 'same distance from A as from B' = perpendicular bisector of AB (compasses open to more than 4 cm, centre A then centre B, arcs above and below AB, join the two crossings). Locus 2 = 'same distance from AB as from AC' = bisector of angle BAC (centre A, arc cutting AB at X and AC at Y; equal arcs centred X and Y crossing at Z; join AZ). They are not parallel (one is perpendicular to AB, the other makes 26.5 deg with AB), so they meet in exactly one point P. Coordinate check with A(0,0), B(8,0): C = (3.609375, 4.7930), cos A = 57.75/96 = 0.6015625, A = 53.018 deg; the bisector is y = x tan(A/2) with tan(A/2) = sin A/(1 + cos A) = 0.49878; at x = 4 (perpendicular bisector of AB) this gives P = (4, 1.9951). P lies inside the triangle (on BC at x = 4 the height is 4.367 > 1.995), matching the question's statement, so the construction is well-defined and possible.
working.(c): Shortest distance from P to AC = perpendicular distance. Since P is on the bisector of angle A, this equals its distance from AB, which is the y-coordinate of P = 4 tan(A/2) = 4 x 0.49878 = 1.9951 cm. Direct check: |4 sin A - 1.9951 cos A| = |3.1953 - 1.2002| = 1.9951 cm, and the foot of the perpendicular is 4.00 cm from A along AC, so it lies on the segment AC (4 < 6). Measured to the nearest millimetre this is 2.0 cm.

parts.note: Setter and blind examiner describe the same construction: AB = 8 cm ruled, arc radius 6 cm centred A, arc radius 6.5 cm centred B, C at the crossing. Verified: the triangle inequality holds (6 + 6.5 > 8), cos A = 57.75/96 = 77/128, angle A = 53.02 deg, C = (3.609, 4.793) with A(0,0), B(8,0), so the drawing is 8 cm wide and 4.8 cm tall and fits an answer space. Key correct.

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both decode the two conditions into the same loci: perpendicular bisector of AB (x = 4) and the bisector of angle BAC (y = x tan 26.51 deg, tan(A/2) = sin A/(1 + cos A) = 0.49878), meeting at P = (4, 1.995). Verified inside the triangle: BC is 4.37 cm above AB at x = 4, and P is 4.47 cm from A along a bisector 6.14 cm long. The key's aside 'PA = PB = 4.5 cm' is 4.47 cm exact, i.e. 4.5 cm to the nearest millimetre; not a candidate answer, so harmless. Key correct.

parts.label: (c)
parts.note: Setter 2.0 cm (exact 1.995, accept 1.9-2.1, follow through); blind 2.0 cm (accept 1.9-2.1). Verified directly: |4 sin A - 1.995 cos A| = 1.995 cm, and the foot of the perpendicular is exactly 4.00 cm along AC, so it lies on the 6 cm segment. The answer is derivable from the stated lengths alone; the band is discussed in fixes.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement on any part; every value in the key is correct and 2.0 cm is derivable exactly from the three given sides (1.995 cm), the only reservation being the width of the (c) band.
fixes: Widen the (c) band to 1.8-2.2 cm (+/-0.2 cm) and keep the follow-through rider: a 1 degree slip in the angle bisector alone moves PM to 1.91 or 2.08 cm, and P also inherits the triangle's own +/-0.1 cm side errors, so +/-0.1 cm is a direct-measurement tolerance applied to a point fixed by two compounded constructions; state it in the key as 'ft their P'.

Optional, to put clearer water between (b)+(c) and GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q7(c) (the same two loci meeting at P, then a measured length), change what is measured to something that uses the constructed triangle, e.g. 'By measuring, find angle APB' (exact 127.0 deg, accept 126-128) or 'the length CP' (exact 2.83 cm, accept 2.7-2.9 with ft); only if the specimen echo matters more than the present bisector-property twist.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 standard as a 4-mark construction item: the triangle is built from three stated sides so nothing is measured from a printed figure, neither locus is named (each equal-distance condition has to be decoded into the right bisector, the decision GCE 2025 P1 Q7 pushes into its part (c) and GCE 2019/2017 leave to a shaded region), and the last mark measures a distance whose value the bisector property lets a candidate read straight off the perpendicular bisector; one idea then three routines, finishable in about 5 minutes, register and numbers exam-clean, no scale drawing, key and blind agree. It re-skins no 2024/2025 question (2025 P1 Q7 names both constructions on a printed quadrilateral and shades a region); its closest relatives are GCE 2011 P1 Q20 (constructed triangle) and the 2023 specimen Q7 (two loci then a measurement), from which it differs by withholding the construction names and by what is measured. Gates pass (jaccard 0.068 to GCE 2011 P1 Q19, 3 rounds); the previous verdict's follow-through rider was applied, its +/-0.2 band was not, hence 4.

question.stem:
The perimeter of a rectangle is 38 cm and the length of one of its diagonals is 15 cm.
Find the difference between the length and the width of the rectangle.
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
question.answer: $9.4$ cm (from $\sqrt{89} = 9.434\ldots$; subtracting the rounded roots $14.22 - 4.78 = 9.44$ also gives $9.4$)
question.solution:
Let the length be $x$ cm and the width be $y$ cm, with $x > y$.
Perimeter: $2x + 2y = 38$, so $x + y = 19$.
The diagonal is the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle on the length and the width, so by Pythagoras' theorem $x^2 + y^2 = 15^2 = 225$.

Method 1 (identities):
$(x - y)^2 = 2(x^2 + y^2) - (x + y)^2 = 2(225) - 19^2 = 450 - 361 = 89$.
(Equivalently, $(x + y)^2 = x^2 + 2xy + y^2$ gives $361 = 225 + 2xy$, so $xy = 68$; then $(x - y)^2 = x^2 - 2xy + y^2 = 225 - 136 = 89$.)
Since the length is greater than the width, $x - y = \sqrt{89} = 9.434\ldots = 9.4$ cm (1 d.p.).

Method 2 (quadratic):
$y = 19 - x$, so $x^2 + (19 - x)^2 = 225$, giving $2x^2 - 38x + 136 = 0$, i.e. $x^2 - 19x + 68 = 0$.
$x = \frac{19 \pm \sqrt{19^2 - 4(68)}}{2} = \frac{19 \pm \sqrt{89}}{2}$, so $x = 14.22$ and $y = 4.78$ (2 d.p.).
Difference $= \frac{19 + \sqrt{89}}{2} - \frac{19 - \sqrt{89}}{2} = \sqrt{89} = 9.4$ cm (1 d.p.); a candidate who subtracts the rounded roots gets $14.22 - 4.78 = 9.44 = 9.4$ cm, the same printed answer.

Check: $14.217^2 + 4.783^2 = 202.12 + 22.88 = 225.0$ and $14.217 + 4.783 = 19.0$.

Mark scheme: M1 for both equations $x + y = 19$ and $x^2 + y^2 = 225$; M1 for the combination $(x - y)^2 = 2(x^2 + y^2) - (x + y)^2$ (or $xy = 68$ then $(x - y)^2 = 225 - 136$), or for the quadratic $x^2 - 19x + 68 = 0$; A1 for $9.4$ (from $\sqrt{89}$, $9.43$ or $9.44$).
Common error: reading the perimeter as $x + y = 38$, which gives $(x - y)^2 = 450 - 1444 < 0$ — no such rectangle exists, so the candidate should be sent back to the perimeter.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 N5 Algebraic expressions and formulae: the identities $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$ and $(a - b)^2 = a^2 - 2ab + b^2$; G4 Pythagoras' theorem for the diagonal of a rectangle; the alternative route is N7 solving a quadratic equation by the formula (roots to 2 decimal places). The exact answer $\sqrt{89}$ is a single calculator square root — no surd manipulation, no completing the square, nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: One unscaffolded 3-mark item with no parts, as Paper 1 asks in 2024/25 (GCE 2025 P1 Q22, Q23). The corpus's identity questions compare coefficients (GCE 2006 P1 Q16, GCE 2021 P1 Q15, GCE 2023 specimen Q8) or evaluate a difference of squares (GCE 2007 P2 Q2, GCE 2016 P1 Q4); no corpus question gives a rectangle's perimeter and diagonal, and none in standard-questions-P1.md is re-skinned. The candidate must form both equations himself (nobody says 'find $x^2 + y^2$' or 'form an equation'), decide how to combine them — the square identities in one line, or the quadratic on the calculator — and pick the positive root; the numbers make the direct route irrational ($\frac{19 \pm \sqrt{89}}{2}$) while the identities give $89$ cleanly.

parts.label: single
parts.note: Both give sqrt(89) cm = 9.43 cm (3 s.f.). Verified: x + y = 19 and x^2 + y^2 = 225, so (x - y)^2 = 2(225) - 19^2 = 450 - 361 = 89; equivalently xy = (361 - 225)/2 = 68 and (x - y)^2 = 225 - 136 = 89. The quadratic route x^2 - 19x + 68 = 0 has discriminant 89, roots (19 +/- sqrt(89))/2 = 14.217 and 4.783 (a valid rectangle: both positive, each shorter than the diagonal, 14.217^2 + 4.783^2 = 225.0); subtracting the 2-d.p. roots 14.22 - 4.78 gives 9.44, which the setter's key rightly accepts and the blind examiner's exact form covers.

verdict.key_verdict: Setter and blind examiner agree on the single part and the value sqrt(89) = 9.43 cm (9.44 from rounded roots) is correct; nothing is disputed.
fixes: State the accuracy in the stem so the key has one value: add 'Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.' (both the identity route, 9.434..., and the rounded-roots route, 9.44, then give 9.4). If 3 s.f. is kept, the mark scheme must keep the explicit 'accept 9.44 from 14.22 - 4.78' line, since a real SEAB key would not leave the two routes landing on different printed answers unannounced.

SEAB register for the givens: 'The perimeter of a rectangle is 38 cm and the length of one of its diagonals is 15 cm. Find the difference between the length and the width of the rectangle.' (states the measurements of the figure rather than 'A rectangle has ... a diagonal of length'); cosmetic only.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 standard for 3 marks: both equations are hidden (perimeter -> x + y = 19, diagonal -> x^2 + y^2 = 225 with no 'form an equation' cue), there are no parts, and exactly one idea is the candidate's - how to reach x - y from a sum and a sum of squares (the square identities in one line, or substitute and solve the quadratic) - with the numbers chosen so the sides are irrational and the identity route is the one rewarded; the routine that follows finishes well inside 1.5 min/mark, and a 'x + y = 38' misread produces a negative square rather than a plausible answer. It shares only a method (sum + Pythagoras -> quadratic) with GCE 2025 P1 Q20(b), whose situation (a square inscribed in a square, behind a congruence proof), target (the two lengths) and integer roots are all different, so it is not a re-skin; the gates passed (nearest GCE 2002 P1 Q9, jaccard 0.043). It stops at 4 only because the unstated accuracy leaves a two-valued key (9.43 or 9.44) that a real setter would have closed with one line in the stem.

question.stem:
$A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ are points on a circle.
The chords $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at $X$.
Angle $AXB = 104^\circ$ and angle $CAD = 41^\circ$.
Find angle $ACB$.
Give a reason for each step of your working.
question.figure_description: A circle (radius about 3 cm, no centre marked) with four points on its circumference labelled in italic capitals just outside the circle. Going anticlockwise from $A$: $A$ at the upper left (at $150^\circ$ from the positive $x$-axis, i.e. unit-circle position $(-0.866, 0.500)$), $B$ near the bottom, slightly right of centre ($276^\circ$, $(0.105, -0.995)$), $C$ at the lower right ($336^\circ$, $(0.914, -0.407)$), $D$ at the upper right ($58^\circ$, $(0.530, 0.848)$). Draw the two chords $AC$ and $BD$ as thin solid lines; they cross inside the circle at a point labelled $X$ (place the label just beside the crossing). Mark angle $AXB$ (the angle at $X$ between $XA$ and $XB$, on the lower-left side of $X$) with a small arc labelled $104^\circ$, and mark angle $CAD$ (the angle at $A$ between $AC$ and $AD$) with a small arc labelled $41^\circ$. Do not draw $AB$, $BC$, $CD$ or $DA$ as chords. Show NO other angle, no $63^\circ$, no centre, no radius, no other labels.
question.solution:
Angle $CBD$ = angle $CAD$ = $41^\circ$ (angles in the same segment, both standing on the chord $CD$).
Angle $BXC = 180^\circ - 104^\circ = 76^\circ$ (angles on the straight line $AXC$).
In triangle $BXC$: angle $ACB$ = angle $XCB$ = $180^\circ - 76^\circ - 41^\circ = 63^\circ$ (angle sum of a triangle).

Alternative route: angle $AXD = 180^\circ - 104^\circ = 76^\circ$ (angles on the straight line $BXD$); in triangle $AXD$, angle $ADB = 180^\circ - 76^\circ - 41^\circ = 63^\circ$ (angle sum of a triangle); angle $ACB$ = angle $ADB$ = $63^\circ$ (angles in the same segment, both standing on the chord $AB$).

Check by arcs: angle $CAD = 41^\circ$ means arc $CD = 82^\circ$; the angle between the chords, $104^\circ$, is half the sum of arcs $AB$ and $CD$, so arc $AB = 208^\circ - 82^\circ = 126^\circ$ and angle $ACB = 63^\circ$.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 G3 Properties of circles: angles in the same segment are equal, used with angles on a straight line and the angle sum of a triangle (G1), reasons stated. No tangent, no centre, no alternate segment theorem (not in 4052).
question.originality_note: The recent 2-mark and 3-mark circle items use a centre with a tangent or a straight line through $O$ (GCE 2024 P1 Q13, GCE 2025 P1 Q16, GCE 2022 P1 Q17, GCE 2023 specimen Q20, GCE 2020 P1 Q3). This one has no centre at all: two chords crossing, one angle at the crossing and one angle at the circumference, and the candidate must decide which pair of same-segment angles (on chord $CD$ or on chord $AB$) unlocks the target and then find the missing triangle angle. The only corpus question with crossing chords (GCE 2008 P2 Q6) is a similarity proof with a right angle at the crossing.

answers.single: Angle ACB = 63°.  Working with reasons: In triangle AXD, angle AXB is the exterior angle at X (X lies on BD), so angle AXB = angle XAD + angle ADX  [exterior angle of a triangle = sum of the interior opposite angles].  104° = 41° + angle ADX, so angle ADX = 63°, i.e. angle ADB = 63° (X lies on DB).  Then angle ACB = angle ADB = 63°  [angles in the same segment, both standing on chord AB].  (Equivalent first step: angle AXD = 180° − 104° = 76° [angles on a straight line BD], then angle ADX = 180° − 76° − 41° = 63° [angle sum of triangle AXD].)

parts.label: single
parts.note: Setter 63 deg via angle CBD = 41 deg (same segment, chord CD), angle BXC = 76 deg (straight line AXC), triangle BXC; blind 63 deg via angle ADB = 104 - 41 = 63 deg (exterior angle of triangle AXD, or straight line BXD then angle sum) and angle ACB = angle ADB (same segment, chord AB). Both routes are valid with correct reasons. Verified by arcs: arc CD = 82 deg, arc AB = 2 x 104 - 82 = 126 deg, angle ACB = 63 deg; and the figure description's points (A 150 deg, B 276 deg, C 336 deg, D 58 deg) reproduce angle CAD = 41.0 deg and angle AXB = 104.0 deg exactly, with angle ACB = 63.0 deg.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement; 63 degrees is correct by both the setter's route and the blind examiner's route, and the figure is geometrically consistent with the given angles.
verdict.why: At the 2024/25 standard for 2 marks: nothing is named, the candidate must supply the one idea (which pair of same-segment angles unlocks ACB - on chord CD via B, or on chord AB via D) and then run the straight-line / exterior-angle and triangle-sum routine with a reason per step, the same weight and demand as GCE 2025 P1 Q16(b) and GCE 2024 P1 Q13(a) but with no centre, no tangent and crossing chords, so it re-skins nothing in the 2024/25 papers; register ('Give a reason for each step of your working'), numbers and position are exam-clean, and the figure description prints only the two given angles and no 63 deg, so the answer is not on the page. Gates: pass (jaccard 0.138 to GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q20, a tangent question).

question.stem:
A shop sells two blends of coffee beans.
In Blend A, the ratio of the mass of arabica beans to the mass of robusta beans is $3 : 1$.
In Blend B, the ratio of the mass of arabica beans to the mass of robusta beans is $3 : 2$.
800 g of Blend A is mixed with some Blend B.
In the mixture, the ratio of the mass of arabica beans to the mass of robusta beans is $9 : 4$.
Find the mass of Blend B used.
question.solution:
The two ratios cannot be combined as they stand; each must be turned into masses.
800 g of Blend A: arabica $\dfrac{3}{4} \times 800 = 600$ g, robusta $\dfrac{1}{4} \times 800 = 200$ g.
Let the mass of Blend B used be $m$ g: arabica $\dfrac{3}{5}m$ g, robusta $\dfrac{2}{5}m$ g.
Mixture: arabica $\left(600 + \dfrac{3}{5}m\right)$ g, robusta $\left(200 + \dfrac{2}{5}m\right)$ g.
$\dfrac{600 + \frac{3}{5}m}{200 + \frac{2}{5}m} = \dfrac{9}{4}$
$4\left(600 + \dfrac{3}{5}m\right) = 9\left(200 + \dfrac{2}{5}m\right)$
$2400 + \dfrac{12}{5}m = 1800 + \dfrac{18}{5}m$
$600 = \dfrac{6}{5}m$
$m = 500$
The mass of Blend B used is 500 g.
Check: arabica $600 + 300 = 900$ g, robusta $200 + 200 = 400$ g, $900 : 400 = 9 : 4$.

Alternative route: the mixture has mass $(800 + m)$ g, of which $\dfrac{9}{13}$ is arabica, so $\dfrac{9}{13}(800 + m) = 600 + \dfrac{3}{5}m$, giving $9(800 + m) = 13\left(600 + \dfrac{3}{5}m\right)$, $7200 + 9m = 7800 + \dfrac{39}{5}m$, $\dfrac{6}{5}m = 600$, $m = 500$.

Marking: M1 for 600 g and 200 g in the 800 g of Blend A; M1 for the mixture masses $600 + \frac{3}{5}m$ and $200 + \frac{2}{5}m$ (or the arabica as $\frac{9}{13}(800 + m)$); M1 for an equation in $m$ equivalent to $4(600 + \frac{3}{5}m) = 9(200 + \frac{2}{5}m)$; A1 for 500 g. The tidy wrong answer 1800 g (taking one part of $3 : 1$ as 200 g and using the same part for $9 : 4$, so $13 \times 200 - 800$) scores 0; adding the ratio parts ($3 : 1$ and $3 : 2$ giving $6 : 3$) cannot reach $9 : 4$ and scores 0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Ratio and proportion: a part of a quantity from a ratio, and combining two quantities that carry different ratios, where the candidate must decide that the masses, not the ratio parts, are added, introduce the unknown mass of Blend B and form the equation without a cue (the hidden-equation shape of GCE 2025 P1 Q20(b) and Q22). The equation formed is linear in one unknown. Answer exact; no figure; no content outside 4052; no 'form an equation' wording.

question.stem:
Solve $\dfrac{9 - x^2}{2x^2 - 5x - 3} = 2$.
Show all your working.
question.answer: $x = -1$ (the root $x = 3$ of the cleared equation is rejected because it makes the denominator zero)
question.solution:
Route 1 (factorise and cancel): $9 - x^2 = (3 - x)(3 + x)$ and $2x^2 - 5x - 3 = (2x + 1)(x - 3)$.
Since $3 - x = -(x - 3)$, for $x \ne 3$ the left-hand side is $\dfrac{-(x - 3)(x + 3)}{(2x + 1)(x - 3)} = -\dfrac{x + 3}{2x + 1}$.
So $-\dfrac{x + 3}{2x + 1} = 2$, giving $-(x + 3) = 2(2x + 1)$, $-x - 3 = 4x + 2$, $5x = -5$, $x = -1$.

Route 2 (clear the denominator): $9 - x^2 = 2(2x^2 - 5x - 3) = 4x^2 - 10x - 6$, so $5x^2 - 10x - 15 = 0$, $x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0$, $(x - 3)(x + 1) = 0$, giving $x = 3$ or $x = -1$.
At $x = 3$ the denominator is $2(9) - 15 - 3 = 0$ (and the numerator $9 - 9 = 0$), so the fraction is undefined there: $x = 3$ is NOT a solution of the original equation and is rejected.

Check $x = -1$: $\dfrac{9 - 1}{2(1) + 5 - 3} = \dfrac{8}{4} = 2$. Correct.

Answer: $x = -1$.

Marking: M1 for either correct factorisation, $(3 - x)(3 + x)$ or $(2x + 1)(x - 3)$, OR for the cleared equation $9 - x^2 = 2(2x^2 - 5x - 3)$; M1 for correctly solving the resulting linear equation $-(x + 3) = 2(2x + 1)$ or the resulting quadratic $x^2 - 2x - 3 = 0$ (to $x = 3$ or $x = -1$); A1 for $x = -1$ alone. The answer "$x = 3$ or $x = -1$" scores M1 M1 A0. Cancelling to $\dfrac{x + 3}{2x + 1}$ with the sign lost, then solving $x + 3 = 4x + 2$ to $x = \frac{1}{3}$, scores M1 only.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Expand and simplify $(2x - 1)(x - 3)^2$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
$P = (2x + 1)^2 - 4x(x - 3)$
Rearrange the formula to make $x$ the subject.

question.solution:
(a) The square must be handled first: $(x - 3)^2 = x^2 - 6x + 9$. Then
$(2x - 1)(x^2 - 6x + 9) = 2x^3 - 12x^2 + 18x - x^2 + 6x - 9 = 2x^3 - 13x^2 + 24x - 9$.
Alternatively, multiply two of the factors first: $(2x - 1)(x - 3) = 2x^2 - 7x + 3$, then $(2x^2 - 7x + 3)(x - 3) = 2x^3 - 6x^2 - 7x^2 + 21x + 3x - 9 = 2x^3 - 13x^2 + 24x - 9$.
Check: $x = 1$ gives $(1)(-2)^2 = 4$ and $2 - 13 + 24 - 9 = 4$; $x = 2$ gives $(3)(-1)^2 = 3$ and $16 - 52 + 48 - 9 = 3$; $x = 3$ gives $0$ and $54 - 117 + 72 - 9 = 0$.

(b) Expand before rearranging: $(2x + 1)^2 = 4x^2 + 4x + 1$ and $4x(x - 3) = 4x^2 - 12x$, so
$P = 4x^2 + 4x + 1 - 4x^2 + 12x = 16x + 1$.
The formula is linear in $x$: $16x = P - 1$, so $x = \dfrac{P - 1}{16}$.
Check: $x = 2$ gives $P = 25 - 8(-1) = 33$ and $\dfrac{33 - 1}{16} = 2$.

Marking: (a) M1 for $(x - 3)^2 = x^2 - 6x + 9$ or for a correct first product $(2x - 1)(x - 3) = 2x^2 - 7x + 3$; A1 for $2x^3 - 13x^2 + 24x - 9$. The tidy wrong $(x - 3)^2 = x^2 - 9$ leads to $2x^3 - x^2 - 18x + 9$ and scores M0; $(x - 3)^2 = x^2 + 9$ leads to $2x^3 - x^2 + 18x - 9$ and scores M0. (b) M1 for $P = 16x + 1$ (or both expansions $4x^2 + 4x + 1$ and $4x^2 - 12x$ correctly signed); A1 for $x = \dfrac{P - 1}{16}$. The sign slip $-4x^2 - 12x$ leads to $x = \dfrac{1 - P}{8}$ and scores 0; taking a square root of $(2x + 1)^2$ with $x$ still on the other side scores 0.

question.stem:
A box contains 2 faulty light bulbs and $n$ working light bulbs.
Two light bulbs are taken from the box at random, without replacement.
The probability that both light bulbs are faulty is $\frac{1}{36}$.
Find the probability that exactly one of the two light bulbs is faulty.
question.solution:
The number of working bulbs is not given, so $n$ must be found first from the probability that both bulbs are faulty.

There are $n + 2$ bulbs in the box. The draws are without replacement, so the second denominator is one smaller:
P(both faulty) $= \frac{2}{n + 2} \times \frac{1}{n + 1} = \frac{2}{(n + 2)(n + 1)}$.
So $\frac{2}{(n + 2)(n + 1)} = \frac{1}{36}$, giving $(n + 2)(n + 1) = 72$.
$n^2 + 3n + 2 = 72$, so $n^2 + 3n - 70 = 0$, i.e. $(n + 10)(n - 7) = 0$.
$n = -10$ is rejected (it is a number of bulbs), so $n = 7$.
(By inspection: $(n + 2)(n + 1) = 72 = 9 \times 8$, so $n + 2 = 9$.)
Check: $\frac{2}{9} \times \frac{1}{8} = \frac{2}{72} = \frac{1}{36}$.

The box holds 2 faulty and 7 working bulbs, 9 in all. 'Exactly one faulty' happens in two orders:
P(exactly one faulty) $=$ P(faulty then working) $+$ P(working then faulty)
$= \frac{2}{9} \times \frac{7}{8} + \frac{7}{9} \times \frac{2}{8} = \frac{14}{72} + \frac{14}{72} = \frac{28}{72} = \frac{7}{18}$.

Alternative for the last step: $1 - $ P(both faulty) $-$ P(both working) $= 1 - \frac{1}{36} - \frac{7}{9} \times \frac{6}{8} = 1 - \frac{2}{72} - \frac{42}{72} = \frac{28}{72} = \frac{7}{18}$.

Mark scheme: M1 for $\frac{2}{n + 2} \times \frac{1}{n + 1} = \frac{1}{36}$ or $(n + 2)(n + 1) = 72$ (the second factor must show the reduced denominator); A1 for $n = 7$; A1 for $\frac{7}{18}$ (accept $0.389$).
Tidy wrong answers: the with-replacement model $\left(\frac{2}{n + 2}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{36}$ gives $n = 10$ and then $\frac{5}{18}$ (with replacement) or $\frac{10}{33}$ (without) — M0 A0 A0; one ordering only with $n = 7$ gives $\frac{7}{36}$ — M1 A1 A0.

question.stem:
$4x + 7y = 34$
$7x = 43 - 4y$
Find the value of $x - y$.
You must show your working.
question.solution:
Rearrange the second equation: $7x + 4y = 43$.
Subtract the first equation from it: $(7x + 4y) - (4x + 7y) = 43 - 34$, so $3x - 3y = 9$ and $x - y = 3$.

Alternatively, solve fully. Adding the two equations gives $11x + 11y = 77$, so $x + y = 7$; with $x - y = 3$ this gives $x = 5$, $y = 2$. Or eliminate by multiplying: $\times 7$ and $\times 4$ give $28x + 49y = 238$ and $28x + 16y = 172$, so $33y = 66$, $y = 2$ and $x = 5$. Check: $4(5) + 7(2) = 34$ and $7(5) = 35 = 43 - 4(2)$. Either way $x - y = 5 - 2 = 3$.

Marking: M1 for a correct elimination step after rearranging, e.g. $3x - 3y = 9$, or $11x + 11y = 77$, or $33y = 66$ / $33x = 165$; A1 for $3$. The sign slip that gives $-3$ (subtracting the other way and reading it as $x - y$) scores M1 A0. A bare answer of 3 with no working scores 0.

All numbers integers; no figure.

No 2024/2025 question asks for a combination of the unknowns.

The full-elimination routes 33y = 66 and 33x = 165 also check, and the sign slip the scheme names (reading -3x + 3y = -9 as x - y = -3) is the realistic wrong answer.

question.stem: Factorise completely $3a^2 + 4b - 12 - a^2b$.
question.solution:
As printed, the adjacent pairs do not group: $3a^2 + 4b$ has no common factor, and $-12 - a^2b = -(12 + a^2b)$ shares no bracket with it. The terms must be re-ordered first.

Re-order so that the two $a^2$ terms sit together: $3a^2 + 4b - 12 - a^2b = 3a^2 - a^2b + 4b - 12$.
$3a^2 - a^2b = a^2(3 - b)$ and $4b - 12 = 4(b - 3) = -4(3 - b)$, so the expression is $a^2(3 - b) - 4(3 - b) = (3 - b)(a^2 - 4)$.

(The other re-ordering works equally well: $3a^2 - 12 - a^2b + 4b = 3(a^2 - 4) - b(a^2 - 4) = (a^2 - 4)(3 - b)$.)

$a^2 - 4$ is a difference of two squares, so the complete factorisation is $(a - 2)(a + 2)(3 - b)$.

Check by expanding: $(a^2 - 4)(3 - b) = 3a^2 - a^2b - 12 + 4b = 3a^2 + 4b - 12 - a^2b$, which is the given expression.

Marking: M1 for a correct re-ordering into pairs that group, with the sign handled, e.g. $a^2(3 - b) - 4(3 - b)$ or $3(a^2 - 4) - b(a^2 - 4)$; A1 for $(a^2 - 4)(3 - b)$; A1 for $(a - 2)(a + 2)(3 - b)$ or any equivalent such as $-(a - 2)(a + 2)(b - 3)$ or $(2 - a)(a + 2)(b - 3)$. Stopping at $(a^2 - 4)(3 - b)$ scores M1 A1 A0. The sign slip $a^2(3 - b) + 4(3 - b) = (3 - b)(a^2 + 4)$ or $(a^2 - 4)(3 + b)$ scores M1 A0 A0. Grouping the terms as printed, $(3a^2 + 4b) - (12 + a^2b)$, leads nowhere and scores M0.

question.stem: Given that $9^{p} = 2$ and $x^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 3^{4p - 1}$, find the value of $x$.
question.solution:
$9^{p} = 2$ gives $3^{2p} = 2$, so $3^{4p} = \left(3^{2p}\right)^{2} = 2^{2} = 4$ (equivalently $3^{4p} = \left(9^{p}\right)^{2} = 4$).
Then $3^{4p - 1} = 3^{4p} \div 3 = \dfrac{4}{3}$.
So $x^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, i.e. $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = \dfrac{4}{3}$, giving $\sqrt{x} = \dfrac{3}{4}$ and $x = \left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^{2} = \dfrac{9}{16}$.
Check: $\left(\dfrac{9}{16}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = \left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} = \dfrac{4}{3}$; numerically $p = 0.3155$, $3^{4p - 1} = 3^{0.2619} = 1.333$ and $\left(\dfrac{9}{16}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 1.333$ (not expected of candidates).

Marking: M1 for $3^{4p} = \left(9^{p}\right)^{2} = 4$ (or $3^{2p} = 2$ used to reach $3^{4p} = 4$); A1 for $3^{4p - 1} = \dfrac{4}{3}$; A1 for $x = \dfrac{9}{16}$ (accept $0.5625$). Tidy wrong answers: $x = \dfrac{16}{9}$ (sign of the index ignored) and $x = \dfrac{3}{4}$ (the index $-\frac{1}{2}$ only half undone) each score M1 A1 A0; $x = \dfrac{1}{16}$ (the $-1$ in the index ignored, so $x^{-\frac{1}{2}} = 4$) scores M1 A0 A0; $x = 9$ (from $9^{p} = 2 \Rightarrow 3^{p} = 1$, so $3^{4p - 1} = \dfrac{1}{3}$) scores 0.

No logarithms are needed or usable (the candidate never finds $p$); no surd manipulation beyond reading $x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ as $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}}$. Nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: Not a re-skin of any corpus item. The 2024/25 indices items put the unknown in the INDEX and match bases (GCE 2025 P1 Q17 $343^{4} = 49^{-5y}$; also GCE 2022 P1 Q23, GCE 2014 P1 Q6, GCE 2009 P1 Q5) or simplify a negative fractional power of an expression (GCE 2025 P1 Q24); no corpus question gives $a^{p} = k$ and asks for a related power, and none then uses that power as the value of a negative fractional power of a second unknown. The gates' nearest neighbour, GCE 2008 P1 Q3 (Jaccard 0.108), is a numerical evaluation of a different structure. At the 2024/25 standard in the 2025 single-answer shape (14 of 27 GCE 2025 P1 questions have no parts): exactly one decision the stem does not name — that $3^{4p}$ is $(9^{p})^{2}$, or $3^{2p} = 2$ — followed by a two-step routine (divide by $3$; invert and square), which is the standard.md 3-mark descriptor; the wrong decisions land on tidy-looking answers ($\frac{16}{9}$, $\frac{3}{4}$, $\frac{1}{16}$, $9$). Nothing scaffolds the chain: the intermediate value $\frac{4}{3}$ is never supplied.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: setter and blind examiner both give x = 9/16 (0.5625), and I verified it - 9^p = 2 gives 3^{2p} = 2, so 3^{4p} = 4 and 3^{4p - 1} = 4/3; then x^{-1/2} = 4/3 means 1/sqrt(x) = 4/3, sqrt(x) = 3/4, x = 9/16, and (9/16)^{-1/2} = (16/9)^{1/2} = 4/3 checks; the M1 A1 A1 scheme with tidy wrongs 16/9 (sign of the index ignored), 3/4 (index half undone), 1/16 (the -1 ignored) and 9 (from 3^p = 1) is sound.
verdict.why: The round-1 fix was applied exactly: the unlinked (a)/(b) ladder is folded into one 3-mark chain with no parts. Gates pass (nearest GCE 2014 P1 Q6, Jaccard 0.115, an unknown in the index of one equation); GCE 2025 P1 Q17 (343^4 = 49^{-5y}, match bases, solve for the index) and Q24 (simplify a negative fractional power of an expression) are different structures, and no corpus item gives a^p = k and asks for a related power with the unknown as a base. Not a re-skin.

question.stem:
$\xi = \{\text{households in a survey}\}$
$C = \{\text{households that own a car}\}$
$B = \{\text{households that own a bicycle}\}$
$n(\xi) = 40$, $n(C) = 25$ and $n(B) = 22$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the smallest possible value of $n(C \cap B)$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the largest possible value of $n(C' \cap B')$.

question.solution:
(a) $n(C \cup B) = n(C) + n(B) - n(C \cap B) = 47 - n(C \cap B)$.
Since $C \cup B \subseteq \xi$, $n(C \cup B) \le 40$, so $47 - n(C \cap B) \le 40$, giving $n(C \cap B) \ge 7$.
The overlap is smallest when every household owns at least one of the two, i.e. $n(C \cup B) = 40$: then $n(C \cap B) = 25 + 22 - 40 = 7$.
Smallest possible value $= 7$.

(b) $C' \cap B'$ is the set of households that own neither a car nor a bicycle, so $n(C' \cap B') = 40 - n(C \cup B)$.
This is largest when $n(C \cup B)$ is smallest. Since $C \subseteq C \cup B$, $n(C \cup B) \ge 25$, with equality when $B \subset C$ (every bicycle-owning household also owns a car).
Largest possible value $= 40 - 25 = 15$.

Marking: (a) B1 for $7$. The tidy wrong answers score 0: $22$ (taking $B \subset C$, which gives the LARGEST overlap) and $0$ (assuming the sets can be disjoint, impossible since $25 + 22 > 40$). (b) B1 for $15$. The tidy wrong answers score 0: $0$ (carrying the configuration of part (a), where the union fills $\xi$), $18$ (taking $C \subset B$, i.e. $40 - 22$, which is not a possible configuration since $n(C) > n(B)$) and $7$ (reading $C' \cap B'$ as the intersection).
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Set language and notation: universal set, intersection, union, complement, subset, and the number of elements in a set, $n(A)$; reasoning about $n(C \cap B)$ and $n(C' \cap B') = n((C \cup B)')$ from given counts without a diagram. No probability, no listing of elements. Nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: Not a Venn-diagram-with-counts evaluation (GCE 2024 P1 Q17, GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q22 print the number in every region and ask for $n$ of a compound expression), not a shading or describe-the-region item (GCE 2023 P1 Q17, GCE 2018 P1 Q7, GCE 2016 P1 Q3, GCE 2008 P1), not a listing of integers with factors or multiples (GCE 2025 P2 Q7(a) and the 2010–2023 P1 items), and not the infinite-set $n(P \cap T)$ of GCE 2008 P1 Q11(b). No corpus Sets question gives only $n(\xi)$, $n(C)$, $n(B)$ and asks for an extreme value; here there is no diagram, and the region counts are not determined — the candidate must decide which configuration (union filling $\xi$; $B \subset C$) produces each extreme. At the 2024/25 standard for 2 marks: each mark is one hidden decision plus a one-line subtraction, the survey context fixes the meaning of $C' \cap B'$ (own neither), and the wrong decisions all land on tidy-looking answers ($22$, $0$, $18$).

parts.label: (a)
parts.note: Both give 7. Verified: n(C u B) = 25 + 22 - n(C n B) <= 40 forces n(C n B) >= 7, attained when every household owns at least one of the two (union fills xi); 0 is impossible since 25 + 22 > 40, and 22 is the LARGEST overlap (B subset of C).

parts.label: (b)
parts.note: Both give 15. Verified: n(C' n B') = 40 - n(C u B) and n(C u B) >= max(25, 22) = 25, attained when B is a subset of C, giving 15; the configuration of (a) gives 0 (a tidy wrong), C subset of B is impossible as n(C) > n(B) (18 is a tidy wrong).

question.stem:
The diagram shows a rectangular sheet of paper with shorter side $x$ cm and longer side $y$ cm.
The sheet is cut in half along the dashed line, which is parallel to its shorter side.
Each half is similar to the original sheet.

The area of the sheet is $500$ cm$^2$.
Find the length of the longer side of the sheet.
question.figure_description: A single rectangle, NOT drawn to scale, with its longer side horizontal: about 7 cm wide and 5 cm tall on the page (any width-to-height ratio between 1.3 and 1.5 is fine; do not make it exactly $\sqrt{2}$ and do not make it a square). Thin solid black lines for the four sides. Label the bottom side '$y$ cm' in italic, centred just below it, and the left side '$x$ cm' in italic, centred just to the left of it (rotated to read along the side or left horizontal, either is acceptable). Draw ONE dashed vertical line inside the rectangle from the midpoint of the top side to the midpoint of the bottom side, i.e. the cut through the midpoint of the longer side, using the same thin weight as the sides. Print the words 'Not to scale' in small italic just below the figure, to the right. Show NOTHING else: no '$\frac{y}{2}$', no '$500$', no '$26.6$', no '$18.8$', no vertex letters, no right-angle marks, no equal-length ticks, no arrows, no grid, no shading.
question.solution:
The cut is parallel to the shorter side, so it halves the longer side: each half is a rectangle with sides $x$ cm and $\dfrac{y}{2}$ cm.

Which side of the half corresponds to which side of the whole sheet? If $\dfrac{y}{2}$ were the longer side of the half, similarity would give $\dfrac{y/2}{x} = \dfrac{y}{x}$, i.e. $\dfrac{1}{2} = 1$, which is impossible. So the longer side of the half is $x$ and its shorter side is $\dfrac{y}{2}$.

Similar rectangles have corresponding sides in the same ratio, longer : shorter the same in both:
$\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{x}{y/2}$
$\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{2x}{y}$
$y^{2} = 2x^{2}$, so $y = \sqrt{2}\,x$ (lengths are positive).

Area of the sheet: $xy = 500$.
Substituting $x = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{2}}$: $\dfrac{y^{2}}{\sqrt{2}} = 500$
$y^{2} = 500\sqrt{2} = 707.10\ldots$
$y = 26.591\ldots$
Longer side $= 26.6$ cm (3 s.f.).

Equivalent route: $y = \sqrt{2}\,x$ gives $\sqrt{2}\,x^{2} = 500$, $x^{2} = 353.55\ldots$, $x = 18.803\ldots$, then $y = \dfrac{500}{18.803\ldots} = 26.6$ cm.
Check: $18.8 \times 26.6 = 500.1 \approx 500$ and $26.6^{2} = 707.6 \approx 2 \times 18.8^{2} = 706.9$.

Marking (M1 A1 M1 A1): M1 for the half sheet's sides identified as $x$ and $\dfrac{y}{2}$ with the correct correspondence, $\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{x}{y/2}$ or $y : x = x : \dfrac{y}{2}$ (or the equivalent $\dfrac{x}{y} = \dfrac{y/2}{x}$); A1 for $y^{2} = 2x^{2}$ or $y = \sqrt{2}\,x$; M1 for combining this with $xy = 500$ into an equation in one unknown, e.g. $y^{2} = 500\sqrt{2}$, $\sqrt{2}\,x^{2} = 500$ or $y^{4} = 2 \times 500^{2}$; A1 for $26.6$ cm. The tidy wrong routes: the same-letter pairing $\dfrac{y}{x} = \dfrac{y/2}{x}$ gives $1 = 2$ and scores M0; taking the halving as the length ratio, $y = 2x$, gives $2x^{2} = 500$, $x = 15.8$, $y = 31.6$ cm and scores M0 A0 M1 A0; the correct relation but the shorter side reported, $18.8$ cm, scores M1 A1 M1 A0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Congruence and similarity: similar plane figures have corresponding sides in the same ratio, applied to two similar rectangles whose corresponding sides the candidate must identify for themselves; area of a rectangle (Mensuration, routine); Algebra: forming and solving an equation from two relations ($xy = 624$ and $y^{2} = 2x^{2}$), a quadratic in $y^{2}$ solved by taking square roots on a calculator. $\sqrt{2}$ appears only as a number to be evaluated, never as a surd to be manipulated. No trigonometry, no calculus. Nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: Not the liquid-in-a-cone family (GCE 2025 P1 Q21, GCE 2024 P1 Q26, GCE 2023 P1 Q18, GCE 2016 P1 Q7, GCE 2020 P2 Q5), not similar containers or solids with a capacity or mass to scale (GCE 2007-2019 bottles, jugs, wheelbarrows, GCE 2009 P1 Q15 spheres, GCE 2024 P2 Q9(c) cylinders), not a model-to-scale volume (GCE 2018 P1 Q11, GCE 2021 P1 Q18), not similar triangles inside a parallel-line or crossed-chord figure (GCE 2021 P1 Q14, GCE 2012, GCE 2006, GCE 2005), and not the two-squares congruence-plus-quadratic of GCE 2025 P1 Q20. No corpus question uses the self-similar (A-series) sheet of paper. Set in the 2024/25 four-mark P1 shape (GCE 2025 P1 Q22, GCE 2024 P1 Q26(b)): one question, no parts, no printed target and no 'form an equation' cue. The one idea the candidate must supply is which side of the half corresponds to which side of the whole (the same-letter pairing gives $1 = 2$ and stops); the rest is routine: the relation $y^{2} = 2x^{2}$, the area, a square root, and choosing the longer side. The wrong decision $y = 2x$ lands on the tidy-looking $31.6$ cm. The diagram prints the labels $x$ and $y$ and the dashed cut only, so the correspondence cannot be read off it. The area $500$ cm$^2$ is deliberately not a standard paper size, so the answer cannot be written down from memory of A-series dimensions.

question.stem:
A florist has a number of roses.
When the roses are tied in bunches of 8, there are 5 roses left over.
When the roses are tied in bunches of 12, there are 9 roses left over.
When the roses are tied in bunches of 18, there are 15 roses left over.
Find the smallest possible number of roses the florist has.
question.solution:
Let the number of roses be $n$.
In every case the last bunch is 3 roses short of being complete: $8 - 5 = 3$, $12 - 9 = 3$ and $18 - 15 = 3$. So with 3 more roses every bunching would come out exactly, i.e. $n + 3$ is a common multiple of $8$, $12$ and $18$.
$8 = 2^{3}$, $12 = 2^{2} \times 3$, $18 = 2 \times 3^{2}$, so $\text{LCM}(8, 12, 18) = 2^{3} \times 3^{2} = 72$.
The smallest possible value of $n + 3$ is $72$, so $n = 72 - 3 = 69$.
Check: $69 = 8 \times 8 + 5$, $69 = 12 \times 5 + 9$, $69 = 18 \times 3 + 15$.
Smallest possible number of roses $= 69$.

Marking: M1 for recognising that $n + 3$ is a common multiple of $8$, $12$ and $18$ (a systematic listing of numbers of the form $8k + 5$ — $5, 13, 21, \ldots, 69$ — with all three conditions checked at $69$ also earns full marks); M1 for $\text{LCM}(8, 12, 18) = 72$ by prime factors or otherwise; A1 for $69$. Tidy wrong answers: $72$ (the remainders ignored) scores M0 M1 A0; $77$ (the first remainder added to the LCM, $72 + 5$) scores M0 M1 A0; $75$ (the adjustment made the wrong way, $72 + 3$) scores M1 M1 A0; $5$ or $2$ (an HCF route) scores 0.

Only integers, prime factors and one subtraction are involved; no modular-arithmetic notation, no algebra beyond naming the unknown. Nothing outside 4052.
question.originality_note: Not a re-skin of any corpus HCF/LCM item. The 2024/25 items are prime-factor manipulations: GCE 2024 P1 Q19 (HCF and LCM of 720 and $N$ given, find $N$) and GCE 2025 P1 Q10 (smallest $k$ making $793800k$ a cube); the same families fill the older papers — smallest $k$ for a square or cube (GCE 2023 P1 Q4, GCE 2018 P1 Q20, GCE 2008 P1 Q17, GCE 2006 P1 Q8, GCE 2002 P1 Q7), $784 \div \frac{p}{q}$ a cube (GCE 2021 P1 Q20), two numbers from a given HCF and LCM (GCE 2015 P1 Q14, GCE 2016 specimen P2 Q5), exactly eight factors (GCE 2013 P1 Q7), the LCM/HCF of listed prime-factor forms (GCE 2011 P1 Q7, GCE 2010 P1 Q10, GCE 2020 P1 Q20, GCE 2023 specimen P1 Q2) — and the contextual ones are all direct LCM or HCF reads: lightships flashing together (GCE 2003, GCE 2008), equal packs of rolls and bars (GCE 2009 P1 Q18), a box filled with cubes (GCE 2022 P1 Q8). No corpus question is a remainder problem, and none has the twist here: the remainders are not equal, so nothing can simply be added to the LCM — the candidate must see that each bunching is the same 3 roses short and that it is $n + 3$, not $n$, that is the common multiple. At the 2024/25 standard for 3 marks in the 2025 single-answer shape: one hidden decision followed by a two-step routine (prime-factor LCM, subtract 3), with the wrong decisions landing on the tidy-looking $72$, $77$ and $75$. Context carries the whole of the information; no figure; nothing cues the LCM.

verdict.key_verdict: No disagreement: setter and blind examiner both give 69, and I verified it - each remainder is 3 short of its divisor (8-5, 12-9, 18-15), so n + 3 is a common multiple of 8, 12 and 18; LCM = 2^3 x 3^2 = 72, n = 72 - 3 = 69, and 69 = 8(8)+5 = 12(5)+9 = 18(3)+15; k = 0 gives n = -3 so 69 is the smallest, and the scheme's tidy wrong routes (72 remainders ignored, 77 = 72+5, 75 = 72+3, HCF 2) are correctly placed.

Register ('there are 5 roses left over', 'Find the smallest possible number') and numbers are exam-clean; not a re-skin of any 2024/2025 P1 item (GCE 2024 P1 Q19 gives HCF and LCM and asks for N, GCE 2025 P1 Q10 is prime-factor exponents and a cube multiplier) nor of the prime-factor exemplars shown; gates pass (nearest GCE 2018 P1 Q20, Jaccard 0.022).

question.stem:
The diagram shows a regular pentagon $ABCDE$ with sides of length 10 cm.
Calculate the length of $AC$.
question.figure_description: A regular pentagon ABCDE drawn to scale with AB as the bottom horizontal side. Going anticlockwise: A at the bottom-left, B at the bottom-right, C on the right, D at the top, E on the left. Label the vertices A, B, C, D, E just outside the pentagon. Write the length label "10 cm" beside side AB only. Do NOT draw the diagonal AC or any other diagonal, do NOT mark or print any angle (no 108°, no 36°), and do NOT print 16.2 or any other length. Nothing else on the figure.
question.solution:
Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is $\dfrac{(5 - 2) \times 180^\circ}{5} = 108^\circ$ (equivalently $180^\circ - \dfrac{360^\circ}{5}$).
In triangle $ABC$, $AB = BC = 10$ cm and angle $ABC = 108^\circ$.
By the cosine rule, $AC^{2} = 10^{2} + 10^{2} - 2(10)(10)\cos 108^\circ = 200 - 200\cos 108^\circ = 200 + 61.80\ldots = 261.80\ldots$
$AC = \sqrt{261.80\ldots} = 16.18\ldots = 16.2$ cm (3 s.f.).
Alternatives: triangle $ABC$ is isosceles, so the perpendicular from $B$ bisects $AC$ and angle $ABC$, giving $AC = 2 \times 10\cos 36^\circ = 16.2$ cm; or angle $BAC = \dfrac{180^\circ - 108^\circ}{2} = 36^\circ$ and the sine rule $\dfrac{AC}{\sin 108^\circ} = \dfrac{10}{\sin 36^\circ}$ gives $AC = 16.2$ cm.

Marking: M1 for the interior angle $108^\circ$ (or the base angles $36^\circ$) placed in triangle $ABC$; M1 for a correct cosine-rule, right-triangle or sine-rule statement for $AC$; A1 for $16.2$ (accept $16.18$). Tidy wrong answers: $11.8$ (the exterior angle $72^\circ$ used at $B$) scores M0 M1 A0; $6.18$ (the base angle $36^\circ$ used at $B$, or $2 \times 10\sin 18^\circ$) scores M0 M1 A0; $17.3$ (the hexagon angle $120^\circ$ used) scores M0 M1 A0; $10$ (triangle $ABC$ taken as equilateral) scores 0.
question.syllabus_check: 4052 Angles, triangles and polygons: the interior angle of a regular polygon from the angle sum $(n - 2) \times 180^\circ$ or from the exterior angle $360^\circ / n$, and the base angles of an isosceles triangle; Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry: the cosine rule with an obtuse angle (or cosine in a right-angled triangle after the isosceles split, or the sine rule). Calculator use is permitted in 4052 Paper 1 and the answer is given to 3 significant figures. Nothing outside 4052.
