question.stem:
A canteen sells three set meals, A, B and C.
The matrix $\mathbf{N} = \begin{pmatrix} 90 & 60 & 30 \\ 55 & 60 & 45 \end{pmatrix}$ shows the number of each set meal sold on Monday and on Tuesday. The rows represent Monday and Tuesday, and the columns represent meals A, B and C.
The matrix $\mathbf{P} = \begin{pmatrix} 3.50 & 2.30 \\ 4.00 & 2.50 \\ 5.00 & 2.90 \end{pmatrix}$ shows, in dollars, the selling price of each set meal and the cost to the canteen of preparing it. The rows represent meals A, B and C, and the columns represent the selling price and the cost of preparing the meal.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find a matrix that shows the profit made by the canteen on Monday and on Tuesday.
parts.answer: $\begin{pmatrix} 261 \\ 250.5 \end{pmatrix}$, i.e. a profit of $\$261$ on Monday and $\$250.50$ on Tuesday

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
On which day did the canteen make the greater profit per meal sold?
Show your working.
parts.answer: Tuesday: $\$1.57$ per meal ($250.5 \div 160$) against $\$1.45$ per meal on Monday ($261 \div 180$)

question.solution:
(a) The profit on one meal is its selling price minus its cost, so the profit per meal, in dollars, is the difference of the two columns of $\mathbf{P}$: $\begin{pmatrix} 3.50 - 2.30 \\ 4.00 - 2.50 \\ 5.00 - 2.90 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 1.20 \\ 1.50 \\ 2.10 \end{pmatrix}$.
The profit on each day is $\mathbf{N}\begin{pmatrix} 1.20 \\ 1.50 \\ 2.10 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 90(1.20) + 60(1.50) + 30(2.10) \\ 55(1.20) + 60(1.50) + 45(2.10) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 108 + 90 + 63 \\ 66 + 90 + 94.5 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 261 \\ 250.5 \end{pmatrix}$.
Equivalently $\mathbf{NP} = \begin{pmatrix} 705 & 444 \\ 657.5 & 407 \end{pmatrix}$ (takings and costs for each day), and the profit is the first column minus the second: $\begin{pmatrix} 705 - 444 \\ 657.5 - 407 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 261 \\ 250.5 \end{pmatrix}$.
The canteen made a profit of $\$261$ on Monday and $\$250.50$ on Tuesday.

(b) Number of meals sold: Monday $90 + 60 + 30 = 180$, Tuesday $55 + 60 + 45 = 160$.
Profit per meal sold: Monday $\dfrac{261}{180} = \$1.45$; Tuesday $\dfrac{250.5}{160} = \$1.565\ldots = \$1.57$.
The canteen made the greater profit per meal sold on Tuesday, since $1.57 > 1.45$ — even though its total profit was greater on Monday.

Marking: (a) M1 for the product $\mathbf{N}$ (first) with the profit-per-meal column $\begin{pmatrix} 1.20 & 1.50 & 2.10 \end{pmatrix}^{T}$, or for $\mathbf{NP}$ followed by the difference of its columns; A1 for $\begin{pmatrix} 261 \\ 250.5 \end{pmatrix}$ (accept $\begin{pmatrix} 261.00 \\ 250.50 \end{pmatrix}$ or the two amounts stated in dollars). Tidy wrong answers: $\begin{pmatrix} 705 \\ 657.5 \end{pmatrix}$ (takings only, the cost column ignored) M0 A0; $\begin{pmatrix} 705 & 444 \\ 657.5 & 407 \end{pmatrix}$ left as the answer M1 A0; the $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{PN}$ (conformable but meaningless) M0 A0; $\begin{pmatrix} -261 \\ -250.5 \end{pmatrix}$ (columns subtracted the wrong way) M1 A0. (b) M1 for both $261 \div 180$ and $250.5 \div 160$ (each day's profit divided by that day's own number of meals); A1 for Tuesday with $1.57$ (or $1.5656\ldots$) and $1.45$ shown. "Monday" from comparing the totals $261 > 250.5$ scores 0; comparing $\dfrac{1.20 + 1.50 + 2.10}{3} = 1.60$, which is the same for both days, scores 0; dividing both profits by the same number of meals scores M0.

question.stem:
A wire model of a solid is made by joining straight pieces of wire, one piece for each edge of the solid.
The total length of wire used for a model of a cuboid with a square base of side $x$ cm and height $y$ cm is $116$ cm.
The total length of wire used for a model of a square-based pyramid with base edges of length $x$ cm and sloping edges of length $y$ cm is $84$ cm.
Calculate the volume of the cuboid.
question.figure_description: Two separate labelled sketches side by side, each with its name printed beneath it. LEFT, captioned "Cuboid": a cuboid with a square base drawn in oblique (cabinet) projection, hidden edges dashed; write the letter x beside one front base edge and the letter y beside one vertical edge. RIGHT, captioned "Square-based pyramid": a square-based pyramid with its apex above the centre of the base, hidden base edges dashed, all four sloping edges drawn; write the letter x beside one front base edge and the letter y beside one sloping edge. Print "NOT TO SCALE" once under the pair. The ONLY labels on the figure are x, y, the two captions and NOT TO SCALE. Do NOT print 116, 84, 8, 4, 336, any volume, any edge count, and do NOT label vertices with letters.
question.solution:
Neither $x$ nor $y$ is given, so both must be recovered from the two amounts of wire, and the amount of wire is the sum of the edge lengths.

A cuboid has 12 edges. With a square base of side $x$ cm, the 4 base edges and the 4 top edges are each $x$ cm and the 4 vertical edges are each $y$ cm:
$8x + 4y = 116$, i.e. $2x + y = 29$. $\quad$ (1)

A square-based pyramid has 8 edges: the 4 base edges are each $x$ cm and the 4 sloping edges are each $y$ cm:
$4x + 4y = 84$, i.e. $x + y = 21$. $\quad$ (2)

(1) $-$ (2): $x = 8$.
From (2): $y = 21 - 8 = 13$.
Check: $8(8) + 4(13) = 64 + 52 = 116$ and $4(8) + 4(13) = 32 + 52 = 84$.

Volume of the cuboid $= x^{2}y = 8^{2} \times 13 = 64 \times 13 = 832$ cm$^{3}$.

Marking (M1 M1 A1 A1): M1 for $8x + 4y = 116$ (or $2x + y = 29$); M1 for $4x + 4y = 84$ (or $x + y = 21$); A1 for $x = 8$ and $y = 13$; A1 for $832$ cm$^{3}$. Tidy wrong routes: counting only the 4 base edges and 4 vertical edges of the cuboid, $4x + 4y = 116$, makes the two equations inconsistent and scores M0; treating the pyramid as having 4 sloping edges only, $4y = 84$, gives $y = 21$, $x = 4$ and the volume $336$ cm$^{3}$, scoring M1 M0 A0 A0; the surface area $544$ cm$^{2}$ in place of the volume scores M1 M1 A1 A0.

No surface area of the pyramid, no slant height, no Pythagoras, no figure. Every number is an integer.

question.stem:
In triangle $ABC$, $AB = (x + 1)$ cm, $AC = (x + 7)$ cm and angle $BAC = 150^\circ$.
The area of triangle $ABC$ is $18$ cm$^2$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Find the value of $x$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Find the length of $BC$.

parts.label: (c)
parts.text: Find the shortest distance from $A$ to $BC$.

question.solution:
(a) Two sides and the included angle are known in terms of $x$, so the area formula $\frac{1}{2}bc\sin A$ is the relation that carries the information $18$ cm$^{2}$.
$\frac{1}{2}(x + 1)(x + 7)\sin 150^\circ = 18$
$\sin 150^\circ = \sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}$, so $\frac{1}{4}(x + 1)(x + 7) = 18$
$(x + 1)(x + 7) = 72$
$x^{2} + 8x + 7 = 72$
$x^{2} + 8x - 65 = 0$
$(x + 13)(x - 5) = 0$
$x = -13$ is rejected because $AB = x + 1$ must be positive, so $x = 5$.
Check: $AB = 6$ cm, $AC = 12$ cm, area $= \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 12 \times \frac{1}{2} = 18$ cm$^{2}$.

(b) $AB = 6$ cm, $AC = 12$ cm and the included angle is $150^\circ$, so the cosine rule gives $BC$ directly.
$BC^{2} = 6^{2} + 12^{2} - 2(6)(12)\cos 150^\circ$
$= 36 + 144 - 144(-0.8660\ldots)$
$= 180 + 124.70\ldots = 304.70\ldots$
$BC = 17.455\ldots = 17.5$ cm (3 s.f.).

(c) The shortest distance from $A$ to $BC$ is the perpendicular height $h$ of the triangle on base $BC$, and the area is already known:
$\frac{1}{2} \times BC \times h = 18$
$h = \dfrac{36}{17.455\ldots} = 2.062\ldots = 2.06$ cm (3 s.f.). (Using $BC = 17.5$ gives $2.057\ldots$, also $2.06$.)
Equivalent route: by the sine rule, $\sin ABC = \dfrac{12\sin 150^\circ}{17.455\ldots} = 0.3437\ldots$, so angle $ABC = 20.10\ldots^\circ$ and $h = AB\sin ABC = 6\sin 20.10\ldots^\circ = 2.06$ cm (or angle $ACB = 9.89\ldots^\circ$ and $h = 12\sin 9.89\ldots^\circ = 2.06$ cm). The area route needs no new angle.

Marking: (a) M1 for $\frac{1}{2}(x + 1)(x + 7)\sin 150^\circ = 18$; M1 for expanding to a three-term quadratic $x^{2} + 8x - 65 = 0$; A1 for $x = 5$ with $-13$ rejected. (b) M1 for the cosine rule with $6$, $12$ and $150^\circ$; A1 for $17.5$. (c) B1 for $2.06$ from $\frac{1}{2} \times BC \times h = 18$ (or from $6\sin B$ or $12\sin C$). Tidy wrong routes: omitting the $\frac{1}{2}$ gives $(x + 1)(x + 7) = 36$ and the untidy $x = 2.71$, M0; reading the area as $\frac{1}{2}(x + 1)(x + 7)$ (no sine) gives $x^{2} + 8x - 29 = 0$, M0; $\cos 150^\circ$ taken as $+0.866$ in (b) gives $BC = 7.44$ cm and then $4.84$ cm in (c), M1 A0 then B0 unless follow-through is allowed.

Degrees throughout; no ambiguous case, no bearings, no 3-D, no figure needed because the triangle is fully specified in words.

question.stem:
A fixed volume of water is poured into a cylindrical container.
The depth, $h$ cm, of the water is inversely proportional to the square of the radius, $r$ cm, of the container.
When the water is poured from a container of radius $4$ cm into a container of radius $6$ cm, the depth of the water decreases by $10$ cm.
Find the depth of the water when it is poured into a container of radius $3$ cm.
question.solution:
$h$ is inversely proportional to $r^{2}$, so $h = \dfrac{k}{r^{2}}$ for some constant $k$.

No single pair of values is given: the information is the difference between two depths.
Depth in the container of radius $4$ cm: $\dfrac{k}{16}$. Depth in the container of radius $6$ cm: $\dfrac{k}{36}$.
$\dfrac{k}{16} - \dfrac{k}{36} = 10$
$\dfrac{9k - 4k}{144} = 10$
$5k = 1440$, so $k = 288$.
(The two depths are $18$ cm and $8$ cm, which do differ by $10$ cm.)

In the container of radius $3$ cm: $h = \dfrac{288}{9} = 32$ cm.

Alternative without $k$: $h \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$, so the depths in the $4$ cm and $6$ cm containers are in the ratio $\dfrac{1}{16} : \dfrac{1}{36} = 9 : 4$. Write them as $9t$ and $4t$; then $9t - 4t = 10$, $t = 2$, the depth in the $4$ cm container is $18$ cm, and the depth in the $3$ cm container is $18 \times \dfrac{16}{9} = 32$ cm.

Marking (M1 A1 A1): M1 for $\dfrac{k}{16} - \dfrac{k}{36} = 10$, or for the ratio $9 : 4$ with $9t - 4t = 10$, or for $d = \dfrac{k}{16}$ and $d - 10 = \dfrac{k}{36}$; A1 for $k = 288$ (or the depth $18$ cm in the $4$ cm container); A1 for $32$ cm. Tidy wrong routes: reading $10$ cm as the depth in the $6$ cm container, $\dfrac{k}{36} = 10$, gives $k = 360$ and $40$ cm, M0; as the depth in the $4$ cm container, $\dfrac{k}{16} = 10$, gives $17.8$ cm, M0; using $h \propto \dfrac{1}{r}$ gives $\dfrac{k}{4} - \dfrac{k}{6} = 10$, $k = 120$, $40$ cm, M0.

No mensuration formula is needed (the relation is stated), no graph, no figure; every number is an integer.
question.originality_note: Not the inverse-square force, magnet or solar-radiation family (GCE 2023 P1 Q24, GCE 2018 P1 Q12, GCE 2007, GCE 2006, GCE 2002), not a percentage-change twist on a power law (GCE 2021 P1 Q16, GCE 2018 P1 Q12, GCE 2008 P1 Q13), not a falling object or braking distance, not mass of a cylinder $\propto r^{2}$ (GCE 2012), not gas volume $\propto \dfrac{1}{P}$ (GCE 2010), not workers and days (GCE 2018, GCE 2003), not the scones of GCE 2025 P1 Q2 and not the paint $\propto$ depth$^{2}$ of GCE 2011 P2 Q7. The pouring of water between glasses in GCE 2020 P2 Q5 is a volume-of-a-cylinder calculation, not proportion, and gives a single depth. The context carries real information, since a fixed volume in a cylinder really does have $h \propto \dfrac{1}{r^{2}}$.

question.stem:
These are the first four terms of a sequence.
$$3 \qquad 7 \qquad 13 \qquad 21$$

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: The $k$th term of the sequence is 211. Find the value of $k$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Explain why every term of the sequence is an odd number.
parts.answer: $T_n = n(n+1) + 1$; $n$ and $n+1$ are consecutive integers so $n(n+1)$ is even, and an even number plus 1 is odd.

question.answer: (a) $k = 14$; (b) $T_n = n(n+1)+1$ with $n(n+1)$ even, so every term is odd.
question.solution:
First differences $4,\ 6,\ 8$; second difference constant $2$, so the $n$th term is quadratic with leading coefficient $1$: $T_n = n^2 + bn + c$.
$n = 1$: $1 + b + c = 3$; $n = 2$: $4 + 2b + c = 7$. Subtracting, $b = 1$, so $c = 1$.
$T_n = n^2 + n + 1 = n(n+1) + 1$. Check: $T_3 = 9 + 3 + 1 = 13$, $T_4 = 16 + 4 + 1 = 21$.
(Equivalently, by inspection: $3 = 1\times2+1$, $7 = 2\times3+1$, $13 = 3\times4+1$, $21 = 4\times5+1$.)

(a) $k^2 + k + 1 = 211$
$k^2 + k - 210 = 0$
$(k + 15)(k - 14) = 0$
$k = 14$ or $k = -15$. $k$ is a positive integer, so $k = 14$.
(Check: $T_{14} = 196 + 14 + 1 = 211$. Equivalently $k(k+1) = 210 = 14 \times 15$.)

(b) $T_n = n(n+1) + 1$. Of the two consecutive integers $n$ and $n+1$ one is even, so the product $n(n+1)$ is even. An even number plus $1$ is odd, so every term of the sequence is odd.
(Alternatively: if $n$ is even then $n^2 + n$ is even $+$ even; if $n$ is odd then $n^2 + n$ is odd $+$ odd; either way $n^2 + n$ is even and $n^2 + n + 1$ is odd.)

Marking: (a) B1 for the $n$th term $n^2 + n + 1$ (or $n(n+1)+1$) stated or used; M1 for forming and solving $k^2 + k - 210 = 0$ (or $k(k+1) = 210$) to reach $k = 14$ (and $-15$); A1 for $k = 14$ with $-15$ rejected (a bare "$k = 14$ or $-15$" loses the A1). The tidy wrong route is to take the sequence as linear from the first difference, $T_n = 4n - 1$, giving $4k - 1 = 211$, $k = 53$: B0 M0 A0. Alternative (listing) route: M2 for correctly continuing the sequence (differences $10, 12, \ldots, 26$) to reach $211$ as the 14th term, A1 for $k = 14$; a list that never reaches $211$, or one with an arithmetic slip, scores at most M1. (b) B1 for a complete argument that $n(n+1)$ (equivalently $n^2 + n$) is always even, or for both parity cases; "the first four terms are all odd" or "it goes up by even numbers" scores 0 unless it is tied to the $n$th term (odd first term plus even differences $2n+2$ is an acceptable alternative argument).

question.stem: $VABCD$ is a solid pyramid. Its base $ABCD$ is a horizontal square of side 12 cm and its vertex $V$ is vertically above $O$, the centre of the base. Angle $VAO = 62^\circ$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Calculate the volume of the pyramid.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text: Calculate the total surface area of the pyramid.

question.figure_description: Oblique sketch of a square-based pyramid VABCD, marked 'not drawn to scale'. The base ABCD is drawn as a parallelogram seen from slightly above (A front-left, B front-right, C back-right, D back-left) and the apex V sits above the centre of the base. Draw the sloping edges VA, VB and VC as solid lines and VD as a dashed (hidden) line; base edges AB and BC solid, CD and DA dashed. Mark the centre of the base as O, draw the base diagonal AC as a dashed line through O, and draw VO as a dashed vertical line with a right-angle symbol at O between VO and AC. Label the base edge AB '12 cm'. Mark angle VAO with a small arc at A between AV and AO, labelled '62°'. Label the vertices V, A, B, C, D and the point O only. Nothing else appears: no vertical height, no slant height, no edge length VA, no other angle, no midpoint of AB.
question.solution:
(a) The base diagonal $AC = \sqrt{12^2 + 12^2} = 12\sqrt{2}$ cm, so $OA = \tfrac{1}{2}AC = 6\sqrt{2} = 8.485$ cm (the half-diagonal, not half the side).
In right-angled triangle $VOA$, $\tan 62^\circ = \dfrac{VO}{OA}$, so $VO = 6\sqrt{2}\tan 62^\circ = 15.958$ cm.
Volume $= \tfrac{1}{3} \times 12^2 \times 15.958 = 766.0 = 766$ cm$^3$ (3 s.f.).

(b) Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$, so $OM = 6$ cm and $VM$ is the slant height of the triangular face $VAB$.
$VM = \sqrt{VO^2 + OM^2} = \sqrt{15.958^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{290.67} = 17.049$ cm.
(Alternatively $VA = \dfrac{6\sqrt{2}}{\cos 62^\circ} = 18.074$ cm and $VM = \sqrt{VA^2 - 6^2} = 17.049$ cm.)
Total surface area $= 4 \times \tfrac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 17.049 + 12^2 = 409.18 + 144 = 553.2 = 553$ cm$^2$ (3 s.f.).

Marking: (a) M1 for $OA = 6\sqrt{2}$ or $8.49$ from the base diagonal; M1 for $VO = OA\tan 62^\circ$ (or an equivalent right-triangle relation) giving $15.96$; A1 for $766$. The tidy wrong route uses $OA = 6$: $VO = 11.28$, volume $541.6 \to 542$, scoring M0 M1 A0. (b) M1 for the slant height of a face, $17.0(49)$, by Pythagoras with $OM = 6$ (or from $VA$); A1 for $553$. Using the sloping edge $VA = 18.07$ as the slant height gives $577.8$ and using $VO$ gives $527$: M0 A0. $552$ from a prematurely rounded $17.0$ earns M1 A0.

question.stem:
$OABC$ is a quadrilateral. $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$, $\overrightarrow{OC} = \mathbf{c}$ and $\overrightarrow{AB} = 3\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{c}$.
The diagonals $OB$ and $AC$ meet at the point $X$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.text: Express $\overrightarrow{OX}$, as simply as possible, in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.text:
The area of triangle $OAX$ is 6 cm$^2$.
Find the area of the quadrilateral $OABC$.

question.solution:
(a) $\overrightarrow{OB} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \overrightarrow{AB} = \mathbf{a} + 3\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{c} = 4\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{c}$.
$X$ lies on $OB$, so $\overrightarrow{OX} = \lambda\overrightarrow{OB} = 4\lambda\mathbf{a} + 2\lambda\mathbf{c}$ for some number $\lambda$.
$X$ also lies on $AC$: $\overrightarrow{AC} = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{a}$, so $\overrightarrow{OX} = \overrightarrow{OA} + \mu\overrightarrow{AC} = (1 - \mu)\mathbf{a} + \mu\mathbf{c}$ for some number $\mu$.
$\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ are not parallel, so the coefficients agree: $4\lambda = 1 - \mu$ and $2\lambda = \mu$.
Hence $4\lambda = 1 - 2\lambda$, $\lambda = \tfrac{1}{6}$ and $\mu = \tfrac{1}{3}$.
$\overrightarrow{OX} = \tfrac{4}{6}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{2}{6}\mathbf{c} = \tfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}$.
(Check on $AC$: $(1 - \tfrac{1}{3})\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c} = \tfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}$.)

(b) From $\lambda = \tfrac{1}{6}$, $OX : XB = 1 : 5$; from $\mu = \tfrac{1}{3}$, $AX : XC = 1 : 2$.
Triangles $OAX$ and $OXC$ have the same height from $O$ to $AC$, so area $OXC = 2 \times 6 = 12$ cm$^2$.
Triangles $OAX$ and $XAB$ have the same height from $A$ to $OB$ and $OX : XB = 1 : 5$, so area $XAB = 5 \times 6 = 30$ cm$^2$; likewise area $XBC = 5 \times 12 = 60$ cm$^2$.
Area of $OABC = 6 + 12 + 30 + 60 = 108$ cm$^2$.
(Alternatively: $OB = 6\,OX$, so area $OAB = 6 \times 6 = 36$ and area $OBC = 6 \times 12 = 72$, total $108$; or area $OAC = 18$ and, since the heights of $O$ and $B$ above $AC$ are in the ratio $OX : XB = 1 : 5$, area $ABC = 5 \times 18 = 90$, total $108$.)

Marking: (a) B1 for $\overrightarrow{OB} = 4\mathbf{a} + 2\mathbf{c}$; M1 for writing $\overrightarrow{OX}$ as a scalar multiple along $OB$ and, independently, as a point of $AC$ with a second scalar (either parametrisation of each line); M1 for comparing the coefficients of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{c}$ and solving to $\lambda = \tfrac{1}{6}$ or $\mu = \tfrac{1}{3}$; A1 for $\tfrac{2}{3}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{3}\mathbf{c}$. One parametrisation with no second condition earns at most B1 M1. (b) M1 for any one correctly deduced area from a ratio ($12$, $30$, $60$, $36$, $72$, $18$ or $90$); A1 for $108$. Reading $OX : XB$ as $1 : 6$ gives the tidy wrong total $126$ (M1 A0 when $12$ is seen); adding only the two triangles on $OB$'s A-side, $6 + 30 = 36$, earns M1 A0.

No dot product, no column vectors needed.
